Pressure (downwards), depression (upwards), traction (forwards) and friction (backwards)
quiz.explanation: These four forces are the pillars of aerodynamics: lift against weight (vertical axis) and thrust against drag (horizontal axis).

quiz.question: Why is the explanation of lift by **Bernoulli** alone incomplete?
options: Lift also comes from the **Air deflection** downwards by the tilted wing, through action-reaction
**Bernoulli** only applies to incompressible fluids, yet air is compressible at high speed
**Bernoulli** lift is only sufficient for curved wings, not for straight wings
The **Bernoulli** effect is too weak to lift heavy planes
quiz.explanation: If only the curved **Bernoulli** profile mattered, a plane could not fly upside down; one must also rely on **Air deflection** (**Newton**'s **Law**s).

quiz.question: Which flight control system replaces direct mechanical connections today?
options: Fly-by-wire
Autopilot
Servo-control
Drive-by-wire
quiz.explanation: Fly-by-wire converts the pilot's movements into computer-processed electrical signals, replacing old cables and pulleys.

quiz.question: What is the role of the ailerons on an aircraft's wings?
options: Controlling roll
Reducing drag at high speed
Increasing lift during takeoff
Controlling pitch
quiz.explanation: The ailerons tilt in opposite directions to rotate the aircraft on its longitudinal axis, which is known as roll.

quiz.question: What are flaps and leading-edge slats used for?
options: Increasing lift at low speed
Increasing the aircraft's maximum speed
Reducing the weight of the aircraft
Preventing turbulence at high altitude
quiz.explanation: By modifying the wing's curvature, these devices allow the aircraft to stay airborne even when it slows down for landing.

title: Why do we yawn?
description: Yawning is one of the most universal and yet most paradoxical behaviors in the animal kingdom. Whether it is a lion in the savannah, a snake lying...
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Yawning is one of the most universal and yet most paradoxical behaviors in the animal kingdom. Whether it is a lion in the savannah, a snake lying in wait, or a human in a meeting, this complex reflex mobilizes an impressive muscular chain, ranging from the jaw to the diaphragm. 

Despite its apparent banality, yawning remains a challenge for modern biology. Everyone yawns, and does so starting from intrauterine life, but the exact function of this gesture remains debated. Long reduced to a simple sign of fatigue or boredom, it is today analyzed by neurosciences as a sophisticated mechanism of internal regulation and social communication. By exploring refuted theories and recent discoveries, this course proposes to lift the veil on this daily mystery.

lessons.title: The fall of the oxygen myth and thermal regulation
lessons.content:
For decades, the dominant explanation for yawning was based on the idea of compensating for a lack of oxygen or an excess of carbon dioxide in the blood. This Theory is today totally **scientifically refuted**. Experiments have shown that inhaling pure air enriched with oxygen does not lead to any decrease in the frequency of yawning, just as increasing the level of CO2 does not cause them. Yawning is therefore not a respiratory reflex.

A new hypothesis, led by the researcher <Andrew Gallup>, postulates that yawning serves <brain thermoregulation>. The brain, an extremely energy-hungry organ, heats up quickly. Yawning, through the powerful stretching of facial muscles and the walls of the <frontal sinuses>, would act as a heat exchanger. By inhaling a large quantity of air and briefly increasing the speed of blood flow to the head, the body would manage to maintain the brain at an optimal operating temperature.

This theory explains why we yawn particularly during transition phases (waking up, falling asleep) where body temperature fluctuates. It is also supported by observations showing that an individual yawns significantly less if they wear a cold compress on their forehead or if they breathe through the nose, two alternative methods for cooling the cranial area.

{A study showed that cockatiels yawn twice as much when the ambient temperature increases, proving that this brain cooling mechanism is not limited to mammals.}

lessons.title: The social dimension and mirror neurons
lessons.content:
One of the most singular traits of yawning is its irresistibly communicative nature. In humans and certain primates, it is enough to see, hear, or even read the word "yawn" to trigger the reflex. 

[contagious yawning people group]

This phenomenon is not a simple motor imitation, but a neurological response linked to <mirror neurons and contagiousness>. These brain cells activate both when we perform an action and when we see someone else perform it. The contagion of yawning would thus be a marker of **empathy** and social cohesion within a group. It would allow for the synchronization of the vigilance states of the members of a tribe: if one individual signals a drop in energy or a need for rest, the entire group adjusts its level of arousal.

This thesis is reinforced by the fact that contagion is stronger between close individuals (family, friends) than between strangers. Conversely, a reduction or even an absence of this response is observed in people with social interaction disorders, such as autism. In children, sensitivity to another's yawn only appears between **4 and 5 years old**, the precise moment when the cognitive structures allowing the understanding of others' mental states are established.

{Studies have shown that our dogs are also sensitive to our yawns. They yawn more often when they see their owner do it than when it is a stranger, proving a form of inter-species emotional contagion.}

lessons.title: Fetal yawning: a growth reflex
lessons.content:
Yawning is not learned, it is innate. Medical imaging has revealed that fetuses yawn as early as the **11th week of pregnancy**. At this stage, the fetus is bathed in amniotic fluid and its lungs are not functional; the hypothesis of a need for oxygen is therefore geographically and physiologically impossible.

Fetal yawning seems to play a crucial role in the development of the central nervous system. By stretching the temporomandibular joints and activating the muscles of the face and neck, it would promote <synaptogenèse>, that is to say, the creation of new connections between neurons. 

It is observed that the frequency of yawning decreases as the pregnancy progresses and as brain structures stabilize. An abnormally low or high yawning rate in the fetus can also be used by doctors as a <biomarker> of neurological distress or developmental delay. Yawning is therefore, above all, a tool for brain maturation before becoming a tool for thermal or social regulation.

{Even though they are much smaller, it has been observed that rat fetuses also yawn at the same relative stage of their development, confirming the archaic and essential role of this reflex in building the brain.}

lessons.title: A function of vigilance and arousal
lessons.content:
Beyond cooling and socialization, yawning fulfills a function of **vigilance**. Contrary to popular belief, yawning does not necessarily mean that one wants to sleep, but often that one is trying to stay awake. The massive stretching of the face and chest muscles causes stimulation of the <autonomic nervous system>, leading to a brief acceleration of the heart rate and a mobilization of the senses.

This mechanism is particularly visible in athletes or skydivers who yawn frequently just before a stressful event or a jump. Here, yawning serves to release tension while forcing the body to remain in a state of alert. It is a true physiological "reset" that prepares the body for action or a change of state.

Finally, it is interesting to note that the average duration of a yawn is about **6 seconds**. During this short lapse of time, our senses are partially disconnected (our eyes close, our hearing is interfered with by the sound of the contracted muscles), which proves that the final physiological benefit must be greater than this temporary risk of vulnerability.

|| Yawning is a complex vital reflex that ensures the thermoregulation of the brain, strengthens social cohesion through empathy, and participates in neurological development from the fetal stage. ||

quiz.question: Which popular theory about yawning has been scientifically refuted?
options: The oxygen deprivation theory
The thermoregulation theory
The social empathy theory
The alertness theory
quiz.explanation: Studies have shown that breathing oxygen-enriched air does not decrease yawning, proving that it is not a respiratory reflex.

quiz.question: According to the thermoregulation theory, what is the effect of yawning?
options: Cooling the brain to maintain its performance
Warming the blood before it reaches the brain
Increasing blood pressure in the legs
Reducing the temperature of the lungs only
quiz.explanation: Yawning acts as a heat exchanger, using inhaled air and the stretching of the sinuses to cool the cranial area.

quiz.question: Which neurological system explains why yawning is contagious?
options: Mirror neurons
The reward system (Dopamine)
The optic nerve only
The primary visual cortex
quiz.explanation: Mirror neurons make us internally simulate the actions observed in others, which triggers the reflex through empathy.

quiz.question: At what stage of human life do the first yawns appear?
options: At the 11th week of pregnancy
Right at birth (first breath)
At around 6 months of age after birth
At the 24th week of pregnancy
quiz.explanation: Yawning is one of the first reflexes observed in the fetus, playing a major role in its neurological development.

quiz.question: In children, when does yawning become contagious?
options: Between 4 and 5 years old
From birth
At around 18 months of age
During adolescence
quiz.explanation: The contagiousness of yawning requires empathy skills that only mature in children between the ages of 4 and 5.

title: How does memory work?
description: Memory is not a simple faithful and passive recording of the past: it is an **active reconstruction** performed by the brain every time a memory...
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Memory is not a simple faithful and passive recording of the past: it is an **active reconstruction** performed by the brain every time a memory is recalled. Unlike a library where books remain still, the brain reassembles data dynamically.

[human brain anatomy]

This complex biological system is both powerful and fragile, capable of storing a lifetime of knowledge while being subject to distortions. Understanding the mechanisms of memory — from chemical Encoding to nocturnal consolidation — allows one not only to optimize their learning methods but also to grasp the profound malleability of our own identity.

lessons.title: The modular architecture of memory
lessons.content:
Modern science has demonstrated that memory is not a monolithic entity, but a set of **distinct systems** collaborating within different brain regions. The first level is that of <working memory>, a temporary storage system managed mainly by the **prefrontal cortex**. Its capacity is structurally limited to about **7 items** (Miller's number), and information disappears there in less than thirty seconds without active repetition.

Beyond this ephemeral stage, long-term memory unfolds into several functional categories. We first distinguish **declarative memory** (or explicit), which includes **episodic memory** and **semantic memory**. The former concerns the contextualized memories of our own life, like the account of a trip, while the latter stores general knowledge and abstract Concepts, like the capital of a country or the definition of a word.

Finally, **procedural memory** (or implicit) concerns motor automatisms and know-how. Housed partly in the **cerebellum** and the basal ganglia, it is particularly robust. It is what allows you to ride a bike or type on a keyboard without consciously thinking about the position of your limbs. This specialization explains why an amnesic patient can forget his name while retaining the ability to play the piano.

{The record for memorizing the decimals of Pi stands at 70,000 digits, proving that while the capacity of working memory is limited, that of long-term memory is virtually infinite through association techniques.}

lessons.title: The consolidation process and the role of the hippocampus
lessons.content:
For information to pass from a volatile stage to permanent storage, it must undergo **memory consolidation**. This process relies on <neuroplasticity>, which is the ability of neurons to modify the strength of their connections. In 1949, psychologist **Donald Hebb** formulated a fundamental Law: neurons that fire together strengthen their synaptic link. This is the biological basis of memory.

**The hippocampus**, a small structure located in the temporal lobe, acts like a conductor during this phase. It does not store memories permanently, but it "indexes" them and keeps them together for the time necessary for their stabilization. Damage to this organ prevents the formation of any new conscious memory, a disorder called anterograde amnesia.

[hippocampus brain anatomy scan]

Le critical moment for this consolidation is **sleep**. During the night, the hippocampus "replays" the neuronal sequences learned during the day at an accelerated speed. This nocturnal dialogue between the hippocampus and the **neocortex** allows the gradual transfer of information to more permanent storage areas in the cortex. Without quality sleep, this transfer is sabotaged, leaving new knowledge in a state of extreme fragility, subject to rapid forgetting.

A famous study showed that London taxi drivers, who must memorize thousands of streets, possess a significantly larger hippocampus than average, physically illustrating the brain's plasticity in the face of intensive learning.

lessons.title: Memory as a Reconstruction and the risk of false memories
lessons.content:
One of the most destabilizing discoveries in cognitive neuroscience is that remembering is not "re-reading" a computer file, but recreating an experience. With each evocation, the memory becomes **labile** (unstable) and can be modified by information present in the immediate environment before being stored again: this is **reconsolidation**.

Researcher **Elizabeth Loftus** revolutionized this field by demonstrating the ease with which **false memories** can be implanted. In her experiments, the simple fact of changing a word in a question (asking at what speed the cars "smashed" rather than "hit") modifies witnesses' perception of the violence of an accident. The brain naturally fills memory gaps with logical deductions or external suggestions, creating total certainty about facts that nonetheless do not exist.

This malleability has major consequences in the judicial field. Eyewitness testimony, long considered indisputable evidence, is now analyzed with caution because it is inherently subject to **memory contamination**. Human memory is not a tool for historical truth, but a tool for biological adaptation intended to help us predict the future rather than archive the past accurately.

lessons.title: Forgetting to learn better: selective dynamics
lessons.content:
Contrary to popular belief, **forgetting** is not always a failure of the system, but a vital function. A brain that retained every insignificant detail (the color of every car passed in the street) would be saturated and unable to generalize or make quick decisions. Memory therefore performs permanent sorting, eliminating superfluous details to keep only relevant patterns.

To voluntarily strengthen a memory, one must fight against the "forgetting curve" theorized by **Hermann Ebbinghaus**. The most effective method is **spaced repetition**: rather than reviewing content ten times in one day, it is better to review it at increasing intervals (one day, one week, one month). This repeated solicitation signals to the brain that the information is crucial, thus forcing its structural consolidation.

Ultimately, memory is the product of a balance between preserving the past and the flexibility necessary for the present. It defines who we are, while remaining a moving matter, constantly reshaped by our new experiences and our interactions with the World.

|| Memory is not a frozen recording: it is an active Reconstruction, distributed among different systems (episodic, semantic, procedural) and consolidated during sleep thanks to the hippocampus. ||

 There is a rare condition called hyperthymesia (or HSAM) where individuals remember every day of their lives with photographic precision, but this ability is often described as a mental burden preventing the hierarchy of information.

quiz.question: Approximately how many items can working memory (short-term) hold?
options: About 7 items, plus or minus 2
3 items
20 items
50 items
quiz.explanation: According to Miller's rule cited in the course, the brain's immediate processing capacity is limited to about 7 units of information.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between episodic memory and semantic memory?
options: Episodic memory concerns personal experience, while semantic memory concerns general knowledge
Episodic memory is unconscious, while semantic memory requires effort
Episodic memory lasts for a shorter time than semantic memory
Episodic memory only concerns strong emotions
quiz.explanation: Episodic memory stores contextualized events from our life (memories), while semantic memory manages facts and **Concepts** (knowledge).

quiz.question: What is the crucial role of **The hippocampus** according to neuroscientific research?
options: It indexes and transfers memories to the cortex for consolidation
It serves as a permanent storage area for all memories
It is solely responsible for **procedural memory** and motor skills
It destroys useless memories to avoid saturation
quiz.explanation: The **hippocampus** acts as a gateway: it processes incoming information and helps its transfer to the **neocortex** during sleep.

quiz.question: What did Elizabeth Loftus's work on memory highlight?
options: Memory is a malleable **Reconstruction** subject to false memories
Memory is an infallible recording if the witness is sincere
One cannot implant false memories in a healthy adult
Forgetting is systematically due to an organic brain disease
quiz.explanation: Her studies show that external suggestions can modify or create memories from scratch, proving that memory is a constant **Reconstruction**.

quiz.question: Specifically, what happens during sleep for memorization?
options: The **hippocampus** replays information to stabilize it in the cortex
The brain stops processing information to rest
The **working memory** empties without transferring anything
Neurons disconnect to erase the day
quiz.explanation: The course states that sleep is the consolidation phase where the dialogue between the **hippocampus** and the **neocortex** perpetuates the day's learning.

title: Why do we get chills?
description: <Chills> are a universal physiological response, but their origins are surprisingly diverse. Whether triggered by a sudden drop in temperature, a...
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: <Chills> are a universal physiological response, but their origins are surprisingly diverse. Whether triggered by a sudden drop in temperature, a sudden burst of fear, or a sublime melody, they testify to the complex reactivity of our body. These cutaneous and muscular manifestations are the result of coordination between the brain and the <autonomic nervous system>, acting as adaptive mechanisms inherited from our long evolutionary history.

lessons.title: Thermoregulation: shivering as a biological boiler
lessons.content:
Maintaining an internal body temperature around **37°C** is an absolute priority for the proper functioning of vital organs. When sensory receptors in the skin detect ambient cooling, they transmit the information to the **hypothalamus**, the brain's true thermal control center. In response, the latter orders **vasoconstriction**, a tightening of the peripheral blood vessels that redirects warm blood to the central organs.

If this measure is not enough, the body triggers **chills**: rapid, repetitive, and involuntary muscle contractions. This mechanical movement is not intended to produce a gesture, but to generate thermal energy through internal friction. An adult in a state of intense shivering can multiply their heat production by **4 to 5** in just a few minutes to compensate for calorie loss.

This thermal process is often accompanied by the pilo-motor reflex, better known as **goosebumps**. In our ancestors who possessed a thick coat, the raising of the hair allowed for the trapping of a layer of still air near the skin, thus creating a natural insulating envelope.

[goosebumps cold skin]

{If birds look like us when they fluff their feathers in winter, it's for the same reason: to create an insulating layer of air to survive freezing nights.}

lessons.title: The survival reaction: adrenaline and muscular alertness
lessons.content:
The chill does not only serve to warm up; it is also a key component of the response to psychological or physical stress. When a threat is perceived, the <sympathetic nervous system> activates instantly, triggering the so-called **fight or flight** response. This biological cascade releases massive **adrenaline** into the bloodstream.

The body then enters a state of maximum alert: the heart rate accelerates to oxygenate the muscles, the pupils dilate to better see the danger, and blood is redistributed to the motor limbs. Chills of fear result from a sudden and uncoordinated activation of skeletal muscles, which prepare for an immediate expenditure of energy.

[adrenaline stress response body]

Evolutionarily, the **goosebumps** associated with fear have an intimidation function. By raising their hair or quills, many mammals seek to appear larger and more dangerous to a predator. Although humans have lost their fur, this reflex remains inscribed in our nervous system, witnessing our animal origins.

The sequence is so fast that the chill often precedes the clear awareness of danger, illustrating the efficiency of our archaic survival circuits.

lessons.title: The aesthetic chill: pleasure through dopamine
lessons.content:
Unlike chills from cold or fear, **aesthetic chills** (or **«chills»**) do not seem to have any immediate survival utility. They occur during an intense emotion provoked by a Work of art, a powerful speech or, most often, music. This phenomenon is based on the activation of the **reward** circuit.

Neuroscience research shows that listening to a deeply moving musical passage triggers a massive release of **dopamine** in the nucleus accumbens, an area of the primitive brain associated with intense pleasure. This process is identical to that caused by the consumption of tasty food or drugs. The body reacts physically to a purely intellectual and emotional stimulation with a heart rate acceleration and skin chills.

It is estimated that about **55 to 70%** of the population is capable of feeling these bursts of physical pleasure. This trait is strongly correlated with **openness to experience**, a psychological dimension characterizing individuals who are curious and sensitive to aesthetic complexity. In these people, the brain presents a denser connectivity between the areas processing sound and those managing emotions.

{Studies suggest that musical chills are more frequent during «appoggiaturas», those notes foreign to the expected harmony that create tension followed by a liberating resolution for the listener.}

lessons.title: Variations and limits: when the chill becomes pathological
lessons.content:
Although chills are normal physiological responses, their intensity and frequency vary greatly from one individual to another. Besides psychological factors, the state of fatigue or general health can modify this reactive threshold. An exhausted person will tend to shiver faster in the cold, because their energy reservoir for heat production is weakened.

In a medical context, a chill can become a warning signal, particularly during **fever**. Paradoxically, while the body is already hot, the hypothalamus temporarily «unsettles» the internal thermostat to a higher value (for example 39°C) to help fight an infection. The body then «thinks» it is cold and triggers intense chills to reach this new thermal target.

At the other end of the spectrum, the total absence of chills in the face of extreme cold can be a sign of severe **hypothermia**, indicating that the organism has exhausted its glucose reserves and can no longer warm itself, which constitutes an absolute vital emergency.

|| B to remember: Chills are reflexes controlled by the nervous system: they serve as a heating system (cold), preparation for action (fear) or a signal of intense pleasure via dopamine (aesthetic). ||

quiz.question: By what mechanism do cold **Chills** produce heat?
options: Rapid and involuntary muscle contractions
The acceleration of the basal metabolic rate
Vasodilation of internal vessels
The release of cortisol by the adrenal glands
quiz.explanation: Chills from the cold are a mechanical activity of the muscles which, through internal friction, generate thermal energy to warm the body.

quiz.question: What is the original role of goosebumps in our hairy ancestors?
options: To create an insulating layer of air to conserve heat
To promote the evacuation of sweat under the effect of wind
To allow pheromones to diffuse better into the air
To facilitate the detection of cold air currents on the skin
quiz.explanation: The straightening of the hairs traps a layer of air that acts as a thermal insulator, a mechanism that has become ineffective in humans due to a lack of hairiness.

quiz.question: Which hormone is released during chills of fear, preparing the body for the "fight or flight" response?
options: Adrenaline
Dopamine
Oxytocin
Melatonin
quiz.explanation: Adrenaline is the ultimate stress hormone, mobilizing energy and muscles for an immediate reaction to danger.

quiz.question: Which neurological pathway explains aesthetic chills provoked by music?
options: The dopaminergic pathway of the reward system
The serotonergic pathway
The oxytocinergic pathway
The noradrenergic pathway
quiz.explanation: Musical chills activate the release of Dopamine in the nucleus accumbens, transforming auditory stimulation into a sensation of physical pleasure.

quiz.question: Why do we shiver when we have a fever?
options: The Hypothalamus sets a higher temperature threshold
The body lacks glucose to fight the infection
The blood becomes too thin under the effect of inflammation
The muscles stiffen to protect the joints
quiz.explanation: During a fever, the internal thermostat (Hypothalamus) is set higher; the body then shivers to reach this new temperature that it considers 'normal'.

title: How does soap kill viruses?
description: The global COVID-19 pandemic has brought back to the forefront a seemingly trivial gesture, but one with formidable biological power: hand...
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The global COVID-19 pandemic has brought back to the forefront a seemingly trivial gesture, but one with formidable biological power: hand washing. While modern medical technology offers sophisticated vaccines, simple soap remains one of the most effective weapons for breaking the chain of transmission of respiratory viruses. This course explores the physico-chemical mechanics that allow a simple soap bubble to neutralize invisible pathogens.

[handwashing soap water hands]

lessons.title: The structural vulnerability of enveloped viruses
lessons.content:
To understand the effectiveness of soap, one must first analyze the microscopic anatomy of viruses. These are schematically divided into two categories: naked viruses and enveloped viruses. Enveloped viruses, which include **coronaviruses**, the influenza virus (Influenza) or HIV, possess a crucial external protective layer for their survival. 

This protection, called the **lipid membrane**, acts as a grease armor. It is not just a physical barrier; it also houses surface proteins essential for the virus to attach to and enter human cells. Without this intact membrane, the virus's genetic material (RNA or DNA) becomes exposed and incapable of infecting a host. 

The fatty envelope is held together by weak bonds between lipids. In their natural state, these viruses are therefore paradoxically fragile. Unlike naked viruses (like the norovirus responsible for gastroenteritis), which are protected by a solid protein shell called a <capsid>, enveloped viruses depend entirely on the integrity of their fat layer. It is precisely this Achilles' heel that soap will exploit.

{The Concept of enveloped virus explains why the flu is seasonal: the lipid envelope is more stable in cold, dry weather, whereas it degrades faster in the warm, humid air of summer.}

lessons.title: The amphiphilic molecule: a molecular gripper
lessons.content:
The secret of soap lies in the chemical structure of its components: the <surfactants>. Each soap molecule is described as **amphiphilic**, which means it has two ends with opposite properties. On one side, a **hydrophilic head** ("water-loving") and on the other, a long **hydrophobic tail** ("water-fearing") but lipophilic ("fat-loving").

During washing, a molecular battle begins. The hydrophobic tails of the soap molecules desperately seek to flee the water flowing from the tap. Upon encountering a virus, they brutally insert themselves into its lipid membrane, like crowbars driving into a wooden partition. 

The accumulation of these molecules within the viral envelope creates such pressure that it eventually **disintegrates** the virus's structure. Viral fats are then captured in the center of small soap spheres called **micelles**. Once the virus is thus dismantled, its components are nothing more than harmless debris that the rinsing water easily carries away. This process is a pure physical destruction, leaving no chance for mutation or resistance for the virus.

lessons.title: Mechanical action and contact time
lessons.content:
The effectiveness of washing does not rely solely on chemistry, but also on the mechanical action of rubbing. It takes about **20 seconds** for soap molecules to effectively penetrate all skin folds and saturate the membranes of every viral particle present on the skin.

Rubbing helps dislodge viruses that adhere to the skin thanks to electrochemical forces. Soap acts here as a lubricant that lowers the surface tension of water, allowing it to wet more surfaces, including under the fingernails and in the finger joints. 

This is the major difference with **hydroalcoholic gel**. While alcohol denatures proteins and also dissolves lipids, it does not physically remove debris. Against naked viruses, which have no lipid envelope to dissolve, the gel is often less effective than soap. Washing with soap indeed combines two actions: chemical destruction for enveloped viruses and mechanical expulsion for all types of micro-organisms.

lessons.title: {Soap has existed since at least 2800 B.C. The Babylonians mixed water, alkali, and cassia oil to create a cleansing paste, long before understanding the very notion of microbes.}
lessons.content: Soap vs Gel: choosing the right weapon

quiz.question: Which viruses are NOT sensitive to the destructive action of soap on their membrane?
options: Viruses without a Lipid envelope such as norovirus or poliovirus
RNA viruses such as influenza
Very small viruses such as parvoviruses
Thermostable viruses such as HIV
quiz.explanation: Soap kills by dissolving the lipid membrane (fat). 'Naked' viruses like norovirus do not have one and are therefore only dislodged mechanically.

quiz.question: What is an Amphiphilic molecule, and why is this property the key to how soap works?
options: A molecule with a hydrophilic head that loves water and a hydrophobic tail that loves fat
A molecule that changes shape depending on the pH
An electrically charged molecule that neutralizes the surface charge of viruses to agglomerate them
A molecule with two active heads that can simultaneously bind to two different viral proteins
quiz.explanation: This dual nature allows soap to insert itself into the fatty membranes of viruses (via the lipophilic tail) while remaining linked to the rinse water (via the hydrophilic head).

quiz.question: What advantage does soap have over hydroalcoholic gel against viruses without an envelope?
options: Mechanical friction and rinsing physically eliminate microorganisms from the skin
The alkaline pH of soap chemically inactivates proteins
Soap penetrates deeper into the pores of the epidermis
Soap acts faster than alcohol on proteins
quiz.explanation: The gel kills on the spot but does not remove anything. Soap, through friction and water, 'unhooks' naked viruses that alcohol cannot disintegrate.

quiz.question: Which doctor scientifically proved as early as 1847 that hand washing saved lives?
options: Ignaz Semmelweis
Louis Pasteur
Joseph Lister
Robert Koch
quiz.explanation: Semmelweis demonstrated that hand washing drastically reduced maternal mortality, long before the germ Theory was validated by Pasteur.

quiz.question: Why are the recommended 20 seconds of friction during hand washing crucial?
options: This is the time necessary for the soap molecules to penetrate and rupture the viral membranes
This is the time necessary for the foam to change color and become active
This is the minimum time for hot water to dilate pores and capture viruses
This is the exact duration of the replication cycle of a surface virus
quiz.explanation: Chemical destruction is not instantaneous. 20 seconds of contact and friction are needed to ensure that the soap has acted on the entire skin surface.

title: The discovery of penicillin (Fleming, 1928)
description: In September 1928, the Scottish physician **Alexander Fleming** returned from vacation and prepared to clean his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital...
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
In September 1928, the Scottish physician **Alexander Fleming** returned from vacation and prepared to clean his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital in London. He discovered that one of his bacterial cultures had been invaded by a microscopic fungus. Rather than throwing away the infected dish, he observed a phenomenon that would revolutionize modern medicine and double human life expectancy.

[Alexander Fleming penicillin Petri dish]

This discovery, the result of chance and an observant mind, marks the birth of the era of antibiotics.

lessons.title: The serendipity of a bacteriologist
lessons.content:
**Alexander Fleming** (1881-1955) was not a researcher with rigid methods; legend has it that his laboratory was in a state of permanent mess. In **September 1928**, he was studying **Staphylococcus**, formidable bacteria causing abscesses, septicemia, and often fatal pneumonia.

One of his Petri dishes was contaminated by a greenish mold: **Penicillium notatum**. Fleming noticed a **zone of inhibition** (a clear zone) around the fungus: the bacteria did not survive in contact with it. He deduced that the mold secreted a substance capable of inhibiting bacterial growth. He named this culture broth **penicillin**.

Despite his initial enthusiasm, Fleming encountered a major obstacle: the instability of the molecule. Penicillin was extremely difficult to isolate in a pure and concentrated form. For nearly ten years, it remained a simple scientific curiosity that Fleming used only to facilitate the culture of certain resistant bacteria in the laboratory.

{The Penicillium notatum that contaminated Fleming's dish probably came from a mycology laboratory located on the floor below the same building, traveling through the stairs or air ducts.}

lessons.title: The Oxford turning point and the urgency of war
lessons.content:
The transition from the experimental stage to a usable drug did only begin from **1938**. Two researchers from the University of Oxford, **<Howard Florey>** and **Ernst Boris Chain**, rediscovered Fleming's work. They understood that the potential of this substance was immense, but that it required expertise in biochemistry that Fleming did not have.

In **1940**, the Oxford team achieved the impossible: purifying penicillin and testing its effectiveness on mice infected with streptococci. The results were definitive: penicillin cured where all other treatments failed. The first human test in **1941** on an English policeman, though tragic (the patient died because the stocks of penicillin ran out before full recovery), proved the non-toxicity and effectiveness of the product.

The **Second World War** acted as a powerful catalyst. Faced with the slaughter of war infections (**gangrene**, infected wounds), the Allies made penicillin production a national priority, almost equal to the atomic project. Unable to produce massively under German bombs, Florey's team went to the United States to seek help from the chemical **Giants**.

[penicillin antibiotic production laboratory]

lessons.title: Toward industrial mass production
lessons.content:
The industrialization of penicillin was an unprecedented technological feat. Between **1943** and **1945**, production rose from a few milligrams to hundreds of billions of units per month. American engineers developed deep fermentation in 30,000-liter columns, replacing the thousands of milk bottles initially used at Oxford.

At the time of the **Normandy Landings** in June 1944, stocks were sufficient to treat every wounded soldier. This medical advance gave a heroic tactical and moral advantage to the Allies. For the first time in the history of conflicts, fewer soldiers died from their infections than from the direct impact of their wounds.

After the war, access to penicillin became democratized, radically transforming the global pathological landscape. Once-deadly diseases such as **Syphilis** or **scarlet fever** became curable in a few days, bringing humanity into an era of unprecedented health optimism.

{In the early days of production, penicillin was so rare that the urine of treated patients was collected to filter it and reuse the drug, as 80% of the dose is excreted by the body within a few hours.}

lessons.title: Fleming's legacy and the challenge of resistance
lessons.content:
In **1945**, the Nobel Prize in Medicine crowned the trio of Fleming, Florey, and Chain. However, during his acceptance speech, Fleming chose to warn humanity rather than simply celebrate his victory. He prophesied that if antibiotics were poorly dosed or used abusively, microbes would eventually learn to resist them.

This premonitory analysis defines the **Concept** of **<antibiotic resistance>**. Naturally, through Darwinian selection, bacteria mutate to survive treatments. Today, the intensive use of antibiotics in human medicine and livestock farming has accelerated this process. **Multidrug-resistant bacteria** now complicate even the most routine hospital care.

Despite this contemporary challenge, the global impact is dizzying: it is estimated that penicillin has saved more than **200 million lives** since its discovery. It opened the way to a whole family of antibiotics (cephalosporins, macrolides) which today constitute the backbone of modern medicine.

|| In 1928, a Petri dish forgotten by Fleming became, thanks to the industrialization driven by the Second World War, the first miracle cure in history, spectacularly increasing world life expectancy. ||

quiz.question: Which bacterium was Fleming studying when he accidentally discovered penicillin?
options: Staphylococcus
The tubercle bacillus
The pneumococcus
The meningococcus
quiz.explanation: Fleming was specifically working on staphylococci at St Mary's Hospital to understand skin and systemic infections.

quiz.question: Why did penicillin remain a laboratory curiosity for ten years after 1928?
options: The molecule was too unstable and difficult to isolate to make it a usable treatment
Doctors at the time considered molds to be poisons
The British government had classified the discovery as 'Defense Secret'
Fleming had not published his results in a scientific journal
quiz.explanation: Although the bactericidal effect was observed, Fleming did not have the biochemistry skills to purify and stabilize penicillin en masse.

quiz.question: Which geopolitical Event accelerated the industrialization of penicillin?
options: Second World War
Cold War
The 1929 economic crisis
The Spanish flu epidemic
quiz.explanation: The urgency of treating infections in wounded soldiers pushed the United States and the United Kingdom to invest massively in production starting in 1943.

quiz.question: What was Fleming referring to during his warning at the Nobel Prize in 1945?
options: The resistance of bacteria in case of misuse of antibiotics
The excessively high cost of the drug for third-world countries
The allergic side effects of penicillin
The difficulty of manufacturing the drug from plant molds
quiz.explanation: Fleming had predicted that exposing bacteria to doses that were too low or too frequent would promote the emergence of resistant strains.

quiz.question: Which ethical gesture by Fleming remained famous in the history of pharmacology?
options: He refused to patent penicillin so that it would remain accessible to everyone
He donated the entirety of his Nobel Prize money to the Red Cross
He asked that his name not appear on the medicine boxes
He tested the first purified dose on himself to prove its safety
quiz.explanation: Fleming felt that a drug capable of saving so many lives should not be a source of private profit.

title: The discovery of electricity and its applications
description: Electricity was not «invented» by man: it is a fundamental force of the universe that we spent millennia identifying, then centuries taming. From...
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: Electricity was not «invented» by man: it is a fundamental force of the universe that we spent millennia identifying, then centuries taming. From the observation of static phenomena by Greek scholars to the implementation of global high-voltage networks, this History is one of a conquest of the invisible. It rests on the genius of pioneers like **Franklin**, **Faraday**, **Maxwell** or **Tesla**, whose Work allowed for the transformation of a simple laboratory curiosity into an engine of modern industrial civilization. This narrative explores the trajectory of this energy, from the sky to our power outlets.

lessons.title: From Greek origins to Franklin: capturing lightning
lessons.content:
The history of electricity begins with a simple tactile observation. Since Antiquity, the Greeks noticed that **yellow amber**, a fossilized resin, attracts light objects like feathers when rubbed with animal skin. This phenomenon, which we call static electricity today, takes its name from the Greek word for amber: <elektron>.

Yet, it wasn't until the 18th century that the deep nature of this phenomenon was understood. In **1752**, the American **Benjamin Franklin** postulated that the lightning observed during storms was not divine anger, but a massive transfer of electrical charges. To prove it, he performed his iconic experiment: he flew a **kite with a metal key** attached to the string during a storm.

[Benjamin Franklin kite lightning experiment]

{Benjamin Franklin conducted his kite experiment in 1752 - but it was extremely dangerous. A Russian professor tried to reproduce it the same year and was killed by lightning.}

Franklin thus proved that lightning is static electricity on an atmospheric scale. This major advance led immediately to the invention of the **lightning rod**, intended to channel these flows toward the ground. A few decades later, in **1800**, the Italian physicist **Alessandro Volta** took a crucial step by inventing the first **electric battery** (the **voltaic pile**). By stacking zinc and copper discs separated by cardboard soaked in <brine>, he managed to create a continuous electrical current, opening the era of electrochemistry.

lessons.title: Faraday and the equations of the invisible
lessons.content:
While Volta's battery allowed for the production of current, it remained limited to low chemical powers. The real revolution occurred in the 1830s thanks to the intuitive genius of **<Michael Faraday>**. Coming from a modest and self-taught background, Faraday understood that electricity and magnetism are two facets of the same physical reality.

In **1831**, he highlighted the Principle of **electromagnetic induction**: by moving a magnet near a conductive wire, he noticed that an electric current was generated in the wire. This discovery is the foundation of all our current technology because it allows the transformation of mechanical Movement into electricity.

[Faraday electromagnetic induction experiment]

The consequences were immediate: if one can produce electricity through Movement, one can build **generators** (transforming the Movement of water or steam into current) and **motors** (using current to create Movement). This symmetry is the basis of heavy industry.

Faraday's conceptual rigor was completed in **1865** by the Scotsman **James Clerk Maxwell**. The latter formulated a set of mathematical equations, **Maxwell's equations**, which unify the Laws of electricity and magnetism into a single force: **electromagnetism**. Maxwell also predicted the existence of radio waves, proving that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.

lessons.title: The confrontation: Edison vs Tesla
lessons.content:
At the end of the 19th century, electricity left the laboratories to take to the streets. It was the beginning of the **« <War of the currents (Edison vs Tesla)> »**, an unprecedented industrial and technical conflict pitting two visions of the World against each other. On one side, **Thomas Edison**, a prolific inventor and formidable businessman, advocated for **direct current** (DC). On the Other, **Nikola Tesla**, a visionary Serbian genius supported by **George Westinghouse**, defended **alternating current** (AC).

[Tesla Edison electric power station]

Edison had the first network installed in New York. However, direct current had a major physical limit: it could not be transported more than a few kilometers without a massive loss of energy in the form of heat. Conversely, Tesla's alternating current could be raised to very high voltages thanks to transformers, allowing it to be transported over hundreds of kilometers with exceptional efficiency.

Seeing himself losing the market, Edison launched an aggressive press campaign to discredit alternating current, presenting it as deadly. He went as far as organizing public electrocutions of animals. But the technical superiority of Tesla's system was undeniable. In **1893**, at the Chicago World's Fair, and later with the equipment of Niagara Falls with AC generators, alternating current definitively established itself as the global standard.

lessons.title: The electrification of the World and new challenges
lessons.content:
The 20th century saw electricity become the backbone of Modernity. It no longer served only for public lighting, but now powered homes, means of transport and, later, computing electronics. This universal accessibility was made possible by the standardization of national networks based on alternating current, but it also created a total energy dependence.

Technological evolution accelerated with the invention of the **transistor** in **1947**, which uses the electrical properties of certain materials to process information. This was the shift from power electricity (heating, moving) to information electricity (digital). Today, the stakes have shifted toward carbon-free production and storage.

{The Serbian engineer Nikola Tesla, despite his 300 patents, died poor and alone in a hotel room in New York, preferring scientific research to commercial profit.}

Storing electricity remains one of the most complex technological frontiers. Unlike coal or oil, electricity is difficult to store on a large scale, forcing network managers to balance production and consumption in real time. The transition to renewable energies and the electric vehicle gives all its relevance today to Volta's research on batteries.

|| B to remember: Electricity was tamed over two centuries: Franklin revealed its nature in 1752, Faraday invented the electric machine in 1831, before Tesla won the war of the currents against Edison, imposing the alternating standard that still powers our world. ||

quiz.question: How does Benjamin Franklin demonstrate in 1752 that lightning is electricity?
options: With a kite equipped with a metal key
By capturing lightning in a Leyden jar
By measuring the electrical charge of the air
By observing that iron lightning rods attract lightning
quiz.explanation: By using the key as a conductor, Franklin was able to observe electrical sparks during a storm, proving that lightning was a transfer of static charge.

quiz.question: What fundamental principle does Michael Faraday discover in 1831?
options: Electromagnetic induction
The photoelectric effect
The Law of electrical circuits
The conservation of energy
quiz.explanation: Induction is the principle by which a varying magnetic field creates an electric current, the basis for the operation of modern generators and motors.

quiz.question: What is the decisive advantage of alternating current (Tesla) over direct current (Edison)?
options: Transport over long distances with minimal losses
Lower danger to humans
Easier production at low cost
More constant voltage stability
quiz.explanation: Alternating current allows the voltage to be stepped up via transformers, which considerably reduces energy losses through heat during transport over long distances.

quiz.question: What spectacular demonstration does Edison organize to discredit alternating current?
options: Public electrocutions of animals to show its "danger"
Short circuits that set entire houses on fire

Demonstrations showing that AC wires cause fires
quiz.explanation: Ready to do anything to protect his monopoly on direct current, Edison publicized the electrocution of animals (such as Topsy the elephant) to frighten public opinion regarding Tesla's current.

quiz.question: Which scientist mathematically unified electricity and magnetism in 1865?
options: James Clerk Maxwell
Alessandro Volta
Nikola Tesla
George Westinghouse
quiz.explanation: Maxwell synthesized the work of his predecessors (including Faraday) into his four famous equations, founding the classical Theory of electromagnetism.

title: The discovery of X-rays (Röntgen, 1895)
description: On **November 8, 1895**, in the darkness of a laboratory at the University of Würzburg, the German physicist **Wilhelm Röntgen** observed a...
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: On **November 8, 1895**, in the darkness of a laboratory at the University of Würzburg, the German physicist **Wilhelm Röntgen** observed a phenomenon that would revolutionize the understanding of matter and medical diagnosis. By discovering an invisible radiation capable of passing through opaque bodies, he broke the limits of human vision and opened the era of internal imaging without surgery. This advance, rewarded with the first Nobel Prize in History, marks the starting point of a radical transformation in clinical practice and the sciences of matter.

lessons.title: The Würzburg accident: invisible light
lessons.content:
The physicist **Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen** was conducting research on high-voltage electrical currents using a **Crookes tube**. This device is a vacuum glass bulb in which electrons are projected from a <cathode> toward an <anode>. In order to study luminescence without being disturbed by stray light, Röntgen wrapped his tube in thick black cardboard.

As he activated the device, he noticed that a screen covered with **barium platinocyanide**, located more than two meters away, emitted a fluorescent glow. Intrigued by this radiation that seemed to pass through the black cardboard, he placed various objects between the tube and the screen: a book, a deck of cards, then a wooden box. Each time, the shadow cast on the screen revealed the internal structure of the objects.

Naming this unknown energy **«X-rays»**, he decided to test the effect on human tissue. On December 22, 1895, he performed the first **X-ray** in History by exposing the hand of his wife, Bertha, to a photographic plate for fifteen minutes. The image distinctly showed the phalanges and a wedding ring floating around the metacarpus.

[Wilhelm Röntgen X-ray hand 1895]

{Upon seeing the image of her own bones, Bertha Röntgen reportedly exclaimed: «I have seen my own death!», because at that time, seeing a human skeleton was inseparable from the image of passing away.}

The image stunned the scientific community because it proved that the human body can become transparent under the effect of these high-energy electromagnetic waves.

lessons.title: The diagnostic revolution and military use
lessons.content:
As soon as his work was published on **December 28, 1895**, the news spread with lightning speed. Unlike many inventors, Röntgen refused to patent his discovery, believing it belonged to humanity. This generosity allowed for the immediate adoption of the technology in hospitals around the World, where surgery—hitherto "blind"—suddenly became image-guided.

Doctors used X-rays to diagnose complex fractures or identify lung abnormalities linked to tuberculosis. Before this invention, locating a foreign body in the organism required exploratory incisions that were often fatal due to infections. With radiography, the surgical act became precise and targeted.

[early X-ray medical radiograph]

The real mass test occurred during the **First World War**. Faced with the massive influx of wounded, the need for rapid imaging became vital. This is where **Marie Curie** stepped in, understanding that transporting the wounded to fixed radiology centers was too risky. She then designed mobile units, the <"Petites Curies" during World War I>, equipped with dynamos and radiology equipment. These trucks allowed for the extraction of shrapnel and bullets on the battlefield, saving tens of thousands of soldiers from amputation or death by <gangrene>.

lessons.title: Fatal invisibility: the price of radiation
lessons.content:
Despite the enthusiasm, the end of the 19th century ignored the **dangers of ionizing radiation**. Physicists and doctors handled X-rays without any protection, often placing their own hands under the beam to calibrate the devices. This prolonged exposure caused <radiodermitis>, severe skin burns that frequently degenerated into skin cancers or <leukemias>.

Pioneers like **Clarence Dally**, Thomas Edison's assistant, died in excruciating pain after multiple amputations, victims of their scientific curiosity. Edison himself, traumatized by the death of his friend and his own visual troubles, abandoned his research on X-rays, stating they were too dangerous to be handled without fear.

At the same time, Röntgen's discovery acted as a catalyst for other breakthroughs. In 1896, seeking a relationship between fluorescence and X-rays, **Henri Becquerel** observed that uranium salts spontaneously emitted similar rays without an external energy source. He had just discovered natural <Radioactivity and early risks>. This discovery would be the foundation of the work of **Pierre and Marie Curie**, who would isolate polonium and radium, also paying a heavy health price for their research.

{In the 1930s-1950s, some shoe stores offered X-ray fluoroscopes to see one's feet inside shoes - without any protection. These machines were not banned until the late 1960s.}

lessons.title: Modern legacy and the structuring of the invisible
lessons.content:
Today, X-rays are no longer limited to the simple detection of fractures. They are at the heart of **computed tomography** (CT scan), which allows for the reconstruction of three-dimensional images of the human body in successive slices. This technology, coupled with computing, offers millimeter precision for detecting tumors or strokes at their first signs.

Beyond medicine, X-ray radiation has become an indispensable tool for astronomy and security. Space telescopes track X-ray sources in space to identify <black holes> or <supernovae> explosions, while airports use these waves to inspect luggage. In the field of Art, experts use radiography to discover hidden sketches under the layers of paint of the great masters.

Röntgen's discovery thus transformed the opacity of the world into an exploitable transparency. It allowed for the understanding that the human eye is only capable of perceiving a tiny fraction of the electromagnetic spectrum. By breaking free from this biological limit, humanity acquired an investigative power that extends from the heart of the atom to the edges of the universe.

|| Röntgen discovered X-rays on November 8, 1895, by accident; in less than a decade, they became the most powerful diagnostic tool in History, laying the foundations for modern nuclear physics. ||

quiz.explanation: It was Bertha Röntgen's hand that was immortalized on December 22, 1895, revealing her bones and her wedding ring on a photographic plate.

options: The very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901

quiz.explanation: Röntgen made History by receiving the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 for his exceptional discovery.

options: Marie Curie

options: He refused to file patents
He assigned his patents to the University of Würzburg
He sold his rights to Siemens
He shared his patents with several governments
quiz.explanation: Faithful to a selfless scientific ethic, Röntgen refused to patent his discovery so that all of humanity could benefit from it at no cost.

title: The discovery of the microwave (by accident)
description: In 1945, at the end of the Second World War, technological innovation was at its peak, driven by the war effort. It is in this context of military...
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: In 1945, at the end of the Second World War, technological innovation was at its peak, driven by the war effort. It is in this context of military research that a banal observation - the melting of a candy - would revolutionize kitchens throughout the World. This discovery, purely by chance, transformed a precision detection instrument, the radar, into a now-indispensable household appliance. This course explores how the ingenuity of an American engineer allowed for the taming of electromagnetic waves to heat our food, moving from a 340 kg prototype to the small box present on our countertops.

lessons.title: Percy Spencer and the spark of chance
lessons.content:
The history of wave cooking begins with <Percy Spencer>, an engineer recognized for his practical genius. In **1945**, he worked for the **Raytheon** company, a pillar of the arms industry. His mission consisted of improving **magnetrons**, electronic components capable of producing short-length radio waves, essential for the operation of air defense radars.

While performing tests near an active magnetron, Spencer felt an unusual sensation of heat in his pocket. To his great surprise, he found that his **chocolate bar** had completely melted, while the surrounding room remained cool. Unlike others who would have ignored the incident, his scientific curiosity pushed him to conduct immediate experiments.

[Percy Spencer microwave discovery radar]

The next day, he placed **popcorn** in front of the device and watched the kernels pop in seconds. He then tried the experiment with a fresh egg which, under the pressure of internal steam generated by the waves, ended up exploding. Spencer instantly understood that he had just discovered a new way to transfer thermal energy, not by external conduction like a fire, but by an internal excitation of matter.

lessons.title: The challenge of miniaturization and cost
lessons.content:
Transforming a laboratory discovery into a mass consumption product was a long and costly process. In **1947**, Raytheon marketed the first model, named the **Radarange**. For the time, it was a technological colossus: it stood **1.8 meters high** and weighed nearly **340 kg**. 

[first microwave oven Radarange 1947]

Its price was just as colossal, amounting at the time to about $5,000, or the equivalent of **$56,000 today**. Due to its size, price, and the need for a complex water-cooling system, the device was initially reserved for industrial kitchens, luxury restaurants, and large ocean liners like the SS United States.

The breakthrough for the general public did not occur until the late 1960s. In **1967**, Raytheon's subsidiary Amana launched the first countertop model, the **Radarange RR-1**, sold for $495. This drastic reduction in size and cost was made possible by the improvement of electronic circuits and the replacement of liquid cooling with an air ventilation system.

{The first customer of the Radarange was a Boston restaurant that wanted to test the fast cooking of hot dogs to reduce customer wait times during lunch service.}

Mass democratization took place in the 1970s thanks to the arrival of Japanese manufacturers who standardized production, bringing the microwave below the symbolic entry-level price threshold.

lessons.title: The physical mechanism of molecular agitation
lessons.content:
The operation of the oven is based on the emission of <microwaves>, low-energy waves that sit between infrared and radio waves. The <standard frequency> of 2.45 GHz was chosen because it offers an ideal compromise: it is low enough to penetrate to the heart of food, but high enough to be absorbed efficiently by <water molecules>.

These molecules are called polar, meaning they possess a positive charge at one end and a negative charge at the other, like tiny magnets. Under the effect of the electromagnetic field that changes direction billions of times per second, the <water molecules> attempt to align with the field. This ultra-fast rotation creates intense molecular friction.

{They are called "microwaves" not because they are tiny in absolute terms, but because they are much shorter than the classic radio waves used at the time of their discovery, which could measure several kilometers.}

It is this friction that produces heat. Contrary to a popular misconception, the microwave does not heat from the inside out in the strict sense, but it simultaneously heats all areas containing water. Materials like glass or ceramic, devoid of free <water molecules>, allow the waves to pass through without heating up themselves.

Metal, on the other hand, is an electrical conductor. The waves induce massive surface currents in it. If the metal has points or thin edges (like the tines of a fork), charges accumulate there until they ionize the air, creating spectacular and dangerous electrical arcs for the device.

lessons.title: A major societal impact
lessons.content:
Beyond the technical feat, the microwave has profoundly changed eating habits and social organization. It favored the rise of ready-made meals and allowed for greater individual flexibility within the home, allowing each family member to eat at different times.

The food industry adapted by creating specific packaging and optimized recipes for this cooking method. While some nutritionists initially feared a loss of vitamins, studies show that the speed of cooking and the small amount of water used often better preserve nutrients than traditional boiling.

Today, the device is present in more than **90%** of households in developed countries. It remains the symbol of an era where speed and convenience have become domestic priorities, transforming a radar surveillance tool into an ally of daily life.

|| The microwave oven was born in 1945 from a chance observation by Percy Spencer, whose chocolate bar had melted near a military radar, leading to the invention of cooking by molecular agitation. ||

quiz.explanation: Metals are conductive; waves create electrical currents in them that accumulate on sharp points, causing electric arcs in the air (ionization).

quiz.explanation: The micro-ondes rotate the molécules d'eau billions of times per second, creating heat through internal friction within the food.

title: The theory of gravitation (Newton, 1687)
description: In 1687, the English physicist **Isaac Newton** published the <Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica>, a work that would radically...
subject: sciences

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: In 1687, the English physicist **Isaac Newton** published the <Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica>, a work that would radically transform our understanding of the cosmos. In a few hundred pages, he managed to unify two worlds previously considered distinct: terrestrial physics, governed by change and falling, and celestial physics, perceived as perfect and eternal. By proposing a mathematical model capable of explaining both the fall of an apple and the ballet of the planets, Newton founded **classical mechanics** and laid the foundations of modern science.

lessons.title: The context: astronomy before the synthesis
lessons.content:
Before the 17th century, astronomy was essentially descriptive. While we knew how to predict eclipses and the Movement of luminous points in the sky, we were ignorant of the dynamic cause. The revolution began with **Copernicus** who, in 1543, dared to place the Sun at the center of the system, breaking the dogma of <geocentrism>.

A few decades later, <Johannes Kepler> passed a crucial milestone. By analyzing the observational data of his predecessor <Tycho Brahe>, he formulated his three laws of planetary Movement between 1609 and 1619. He demonstrated in particular that planets do not rotate in perfect circles, but along **elliptical orbits**. However, Kepler himself did not understand what physical engine forced the planets to follow these precise trajectories.

Simultaneously, in Italy, **Galileo** studied the Movement of objects on Earth. He was the first to theorize the **isochronism** of falling bodies: in a vacuum, a feather and a lead ball hit the ground simultaneously. He thus laid the foundations of modern dynamics, but he lacked the link to escape the Earth's atmosphere. The fundamental question remained: is there an invisible force connecting all objects in the universe?

{Newton wrote more texts on alchemy and biblical interpretation of the Temple of Solomon than on physics or mathematics, disciplines for which he is nonetheless world-famous.}

lessons.title: The law of universal gravitation
lessons.content:
The anecdote of the apple, though often simplified, possesses a kernel of historical truth. It was during a forced stay at his family home because of the plague (1665-1666) that Newton observed a fruit fall in his garden at Woolsthorpe. His genius was not discovering that objects fall, but wondering if the force that attracts the apple could not extend all the way to the Moon.

[Isaac Newton apple tree Woolsthorpe]

His **Law of universal gravitation** stipulates that every body possessing a mass exerts an attractive force on every other body. This force is proportional to the **product of their masses** and inversely proportional to the **Square of the distance** separating them. Mathematically, this means that if two objects move twice their initial distance apart, the attraction between them is divided by four.

This Law is an unprecedented unification. Newton demonstrated that the Moon is actually in 'permanent fall' around the Earth: its lateral speed prevents it from crashing, but gravity keeps it in its orbit. He proved mathematically that this mutual attraction imposes on the planets the elliptical shapes that Kepler had observed empirically.

[planets orbit solar system gravity]

By reconciling heaven and earth under a single equation, Newton gave birth to the idea of a **mechanical universe**, predictable and ordered like a giant clock of which God would be the great architect.

{Outside of his research, Newton was Master of the Royal Mint and pursued counterfeiters with such rigor that he had several of them hanged.}

lessons.title: The three laws of movement and classical mechanics
lessons.content:
To structure his theory of gravitation, Newton had to define the fundamental rules of Movement, known today as **Newton's laws**. The first is the principle of **Inertia**: a body only changes its state of Movement if an external force is exerted upon it. The second establishes the fundamental relationship of dynamics: force is equal to the product of mass times acceleration (**F=ma**). Finally, the third Law poses the principle of **action and reaction**: every force exerted by a body A on a body B generates an equal and opposite force from body B on body A.

These principles founded **classical mechanics**, which reigned supreme over the sciences for more than two centuries. Thanks to them, humanity was able not only to understand the cosmos but also to transform the Earth. All structural calculations for bridges, the design of engines during the industrial revolution, and even the trajectory calculations for military ballistics rely on these Newtonian foundations.

The effectiveness of Newton's model was such that in the 19th century, the astronomer Urbain Le Verrier was able to predict the existence of an unknown planet, **Neptune**, simply by observing the gravitational perturbations experienced by Uranus. This discovery was the ultimate triumph of Newtonian physics.

{In 1816, one of Newton's teeth was sold at auction for the modern equivalent of $35,000; the buyer had it mounted on a ring.}

lessons.title: Legacy and limits of the Newtonian vision
lessons.content:
Despite its extraordinary precision at the human and planetary scale, Newton's Theory presented a major conceptual flaw: it did not explain the *mechanism* of gravity. Newton himself said: 'I frame no hypotheses' (<Hypotheses non fingo>). He noted the force but could not explain how such an attraction could act instantaneously across the vacuum of space.

It was the revolution of **relativistic gravitation (Einstein)** at the beginning of the 20th century that brought the answer. <Albert Einstein> understood that gravity is not an 'invisible force' acting at a distance, but a modification of the geometry of space itself. The mass of a celestial body curves the fabric of space-time, like a bowling ball would deform a stretched tablecloth, forcing Other objects to follow these curves.

Today, while we use Newtonian mechanics to send probes to explore the solar system, we must use Einstein's corrections for the daily operation of our **GPS**. Newton's Theory has therefore not become 'false'; it has simply become a special case of a broader physical reality, valid as long as masses are not too massive and speeds are well below that of light.

{Although Einstein modernized gravity, NASA engineers used only Newton's equations to calculate Apollo 11's trajectory to the Moon.}

|| Newton published in 1687 a single Law that explains both the fall of an apple and the Movement of planets thanks to the laws of classical mechanics. ||

quiz.question: What crucial observation had Galileo made before Newton regarding falling bodies?
options: Bodies fall at the same speed regardless of their mass
Falling speed is proportional to the distance traveled
