options: About 1 million
Nearly 100,000
More than 100 million
About 500,000
quiz.explanation: The IPBES global assessment report warned that one million animal and plant species are at risk of imminent extinction.

title: The circular economy
description: The **circular economy** represents a fundamental paradigm shift in the face of the depletion of planetary resources. While our current production...
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: The **circular economy** represents a fundamental paradigm shift in the face of the depletion of planetary resources. While our current production system relies mostly on a one-way flow, this model aims to decouple economic growth from the consumption of non-renewable resources. Inspired by natural ecosystems where the concept of "waste" does not exist, the circular economy seeks to maintain the value of products and materials for as long as possible within the economic cycle. This approach is not limited to simple recycling but involves a total overhaul of the design, distribution, and consumption of goods.

lessons.title: The linear model and the resource dead-end
lessons.content:
The modern industrial economy was built on a model described as **linear**, summarized by the triptych "take-make-dispose". In this system, raw materials are taken from nature to create products which, once they reach the end of their life or fashion cycle, are turned into waste.

[landfill waste garbage linear economy]

This operation relies on the illusion of infinite resources and an unlimited capacity of the biosphere to absorb pollution. However, we are now reaching critical physical limits. It is estimated that the global economy consumes the equivalent of 1.7 planets in biological resources each year. This overconsumption leads to a rapid depletion of **natural resources**, especially strategic metals. <Lithium>, cobalt, or rare earths, essential for digital technologies and the energy transition, could experience major supply tensions as early as 2040.

Beyond the upstream, the downstream of the linear cycle is saturating. Every year, about **8 million tons** of plastic end up in the oceans, degrading marine ecosystems for centuries. The linear model generates a massive negative externality: the cost of waste management and pollution cleanup is almost never integrated into the initial sale price of the product.

{Only 9% of all plastic ever produced by humanity has been recycled; the rest lingers in the environment or landfills for the next 450 years.}

lessons.title: The hierarchy of loops: from eco-design to recycling
lessons.content:
To break away from linearity, the circular economy proposes an organization of nested loops, always prioritizing the shortest cycle as it best preserves the energy and material already invested. At the top of this hierarchy is **eco-design**. This involves integrating environmental impact right from the drawing board, choosing durable materials and facilitating future disassembly.

The first operational loop is **reuse**, which allows an object to change owners without transformation (second-hand market). Next comes **repair and refurbishment**, aiming to restore the functionality of a faulty product to extend its use. These steps are crucial because they directly combat **planned obsolescence**, the practice of deliberately shortening the lifespan of a good.

[recycling sorting waste materials]

**Recycling** is a last resort. While essential, it remains energy-intensive: recycling aluminum consumes 95% less energy than extracting it from virgin ore (**Bauxite**), but it remains less efficient than reusing a returnable bottle. Finally, **industrial symbiosis** pushes logic to the territorial level: heat or material waste from one factory becomes the energy or input for a neighboring factory, creating a true <industrial ecosystem>.

lessons.title: Economic hurdles and regulatory levers
lessons.content:
Despite its ecological relevance, the circular transition faces structural barriers. The main obstacle is financial: the linear model is often **cheaper in the short term**. Extracting virgin material is frequently more profitable than collecting, sorting, and treating complex waste, especially when raw material prices are low or environmental costs are not taxed.

In response to these market failures, public authorities are intervening more and more vigorously. The European Union has deployed a **Circular Economy Action Plan** (2020) that imposes increasingly strict sustainability standards. One of the pillars of this strategy is the fight against the impossibility of repairing electronic objects.

[repair right electronics reuse]

Strengthening the "right to repair" now obliges manufacturers to make spare parts available for several years and to provide disassembly instructions. At the same time, <Extended Producer Responsibility> (EPR) transfers the cost of waste management to manufacturers, financially incentivizing them to design less polluting products. These regulations are gradually transforming business models: moving from the sale of a product (ownership) to the sale of a use (rental or <functional economy>).

lessons.title: Toward a resource civilization
lessons.content:
The stakes of the circular economy go beyond simple technical waste management; it is about building a society of sobriety and resilience. By reducing our dependence on raw material imports, this model offers a form of strategic security in a geopolitically unstable world. The transition however requires a global standardization effort so that materials can be tracked and reused everywhere on the globe via <digital product passports>.

The success of this mutation ultimately rests on the citizen-consumer. The adoption of **The 3Rs rule (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle)** requires changing our consumption habits. Reducing means, above all, questioning the act of purchasing. While recycling is the most visible step, it is reduction at the source that possesses the strongest lever for climate preservation.

{There is currently more gold in a ton of used smartphone motherboards than in a ton of ore extracted from a traditional gold mine.}

|| À retenir : The circular economy aims to break the exhausting cycle of "extract-make-discard" by maintaining resources within the economy via eco-design, repair and recycling, in order to respect the physical limits of our planet. ||

quiz.question: What is the fundamental difference between the linear economic model and the circular model?
options: The linear follow the take-make-dispose cycle while the circular keeps resources in a loop.
The linear model prohibits the recycling of metals.
The circular model is based solely on services being free of charge.
The linear model depends only on renewable energy.
quiz.explanation: The linear model is a unidirectional flow that systematically ends in waste, whereas the circular model seeks to reinject materials and Object into the economic circuit.

quiz.question: Why is repair considered more effective than recycling in the circular hierarchy?
options: Because it preserves the energy and added value already invested in the finished Object.
Because recycling is prohibited by European regulations.
Because repairing an Object consumes absolutely no resources.
Because recycled Object are always of lower quality.
quiz.explanation: Recycling requires crushing and melting down the material, which consumes a lot of energy. Repair maintains the Object in its useful form, thus preserving all the initial manufacturing work.

quiz.question: What is eco-design within the framework of The circular economy?
options: Anticipating the end-of-life and the impact of a product right from its design phase.
Adding green labels to polluting products.
Manufacturing products solely from wood and cotton.
Limiting advertising for electronic products.
quiz.explanation: Eco-design intervenes upstream to ensure that the product will be durable, easily dismantled, and composed of recyclable materials.

quiz.question: What major obstacle slows down the widespread recycling of raw materials?
options: The cost of extracting virgin materials is often lower than that of sorting and recycling.
It is physically impossible to recycle metals like aluminum.
Recycling consumes more raw material than it produces.
Consumers are opposed to the principle of selective sorting.
quiz.explanation: The linear model remains economically dominant because raw material prices often do not integrate the environmental cost of their extraction, making recycling less competitive.

quiz.question: What is the main function of the "right to repair" promoted by the EU?
options: Compelling manufacturers to provide spare parts and manuals to extend the life of goods.
Allowing customers to get a refund for any product after 5 years.
Banning the sale of new products as soon as a second-hand market exists.
Making repairs free for all citizens without any conditions.
quiz.explanation: The right to repair fights against Planned obsolescence by guaranteeing access to necessary resources (parts, blueprints) to repair devices rather than throwing them away.

title: Why are bees vital?
description: The **bees** are not just simple honey-producing insects; they constitute one of the invisible pillars of global food security and the balance of...
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: The **bees** are not just simple honey-producing insects; they constitute one of the invisible pillars of global food security and the balance of ecosystems. True nature engineers, they ensure the reproduction of a vast majority of flowering plants, a service whose value is estimated in the hundreds of billions of dollars. Yet, for some decades now, these environmental sentinels have been facing an unprecedented collapse of their populations. Understanding the mechanisms of **pollination** and the roots of the entomofauna decline is crucial today to apprehend the challenges of sustainable development and human survival.

lessons.title: Pollination: a biological and economic driver
lessons.content:
The primary role of bees lies in **pollination**, a biological process by which pollen (male gametes) is transported to the stigma (the female organ) of a flower. Although wind or water can provide this transport, the majority of flowering plants rely on animal vectors. Bees, while foraging to collect the nectar and pollen necessary for their colony, involuntarily perform this vital function.

[honey bee pollinating flower closeup]

{A bee can visit up to 700 flowers a day. To produce only 500 grams of honey, a colony must travel a distance equivalent to three times the circumference of the Earth.}

The impact of this ecosystem service on our food supply is colossal. Approximately **75% of global food crops** depend, at least partially, on the activity of pollinators. This concerns basic products like coffee and cocoa, but also high nutritional value crops like apples, almonds or avocados. 

Beyond the biological aspect, pollination is a major financial issue. It is estimated that its contribution to the global economy is between **235 and 577 billion dollars per year**. A mass disappearance of bees would force farmers to resort to manual pollination - already practiced in parts of China - which would lead to an explosion in food prices and a drastic drop in the diversity of our plates.

lessons.title: Colony collapse: a multifactorial crisis
lessons.content:
The decline of bees is not caused by a single factor, but by a synergy of threats acting simultaneously. Since the 1990s, beekeepers have observed alarming winter mortality rates, sometimes reaching **30 to 50%** of colonies, whereas the natural threshold is around 10%. This phenomenon of sudden disappearance is often referred to as <colony collapse disorder>.

Chemical substances from intensive agriculture play a leading role. **Neonicotinoids**, a class of systemic insecticides, are particularly incriminated. Unlike surface treatments, they permeate the entire plant, ending up in the nectar and pollen. Even at low doses, they disorient bees, preventing them from finding their hive, and weaken their immune system.

[neonicotinoid pesticide spraying field]

To this chemical pressure is added a biological threat: **varroa destructor**. This parasitic mite sucks the hemolymph (insect blood) of bees and transmits deadly viruses at the heart of the colony. Finally, urbanization and monoculture reduce floral biodiversity, creating 'food deserts' where bees no longer find the varied nutrients necessary for their survival. Climate change completes this picture by shifting flowering periods relative to insect arousal cycles.

lessons.title: The misunderstood importance of wild diversity
lessons.content:
When we talk about bees, we often think of the honeybee (*Apis mellifera*). However, it is only the tip of the iceberg. There are more than **20,000 species** of wild bees across the globe, including bumblebees, mason bees or carpenter bees. Unlike their domestic cousins, most are solitary and do not produce honey, but their ecological role is just as fundamental.

[wild bumblebee species diversity]

{Some flowers, like those of the tomato, require a specific vibration to release their pollen. Honeybees do not know how to do it, unlike bumblebees which practice 'vibration pollination' or <sonication>.}

These wild species are often specialists: they have co-evolved with specific plants that they are the only ones able to fertilize effectively. Unfortunately, they are even more vulnerable than the honeybee because they do not benefit from any veterinary or human monitoring. The disappearance of this diversity weakens the entire food chain, as many birds and small mammals depend on berries and seeds resulting from this wild pollination.

lessons.title: Toward a sustainable ecological transition
lessons.content:
The survival of bees now depends on structural changes in our land management and agriculture. The drastic reduction in the use of pesticides is the first lever of action. The European Union in fact reached a historical milestone in 2018 with the ban of three major **neonicotinoids** in open fields. In parallel, the rehabilitation of **agroecological infrastructures** - such as hedges, grass strips and flower fallows - allows for the recreation of biodiversity corridors.

At the citizen level, the fight against population collapse involves simple but effective gestures. Planting local nectar-rich species in urban gardens or delaying lawn mowing offers crucial refuges in times of floral scarcity. Awareness is global: bees have become the symbol of the fragility of our production system.

Protecting pollinators is not just about preserving nature, but a long-term survival strategy for humanity. By protecting the bee, we protect the very basis of life on Earth: the capacity of plants to regenerate and feed us.

|| À retenir : Bees and the 20,000 species of wild pollinators ensure the reproduction of 75% of global food crops. Their decline, caused by a synergy of pesticides, parasites and habitat loss, directly threatens global food security and the world economy. ||

options: Neonicotinoids

quiz.explanation: Neonicotinoids are systemic pesticides that contaminate the entire plant, disorienting bees and weakening their immune system, which led to their restriction.

options: 30 to 50% per year

quiz.explanation: The course mentions that winter losses reach 30 to 50% in certain regions, which is three to five times the natural mortality rate.

options: 20,000 species
500 species
5,000 species
100,000 species
quiz.explanation: There are approximately 20,000 species of wild bees (bumblebees, mason bees, etc.), many of which are solitary and play a crucial role because the honeybee cannot pollinate everything alone.

options: Varroa destructor
The Asian hornet
American foulbrood
The small hive beetle
quiz.explanation: The Varroa destructor is a mite that parasites bees by sucking their hemolymph and spreading viruses within the colony.

quiz.explanation: According to the course, about 75% of global crops rely on animal **pollination** to ensure efficient and varied production.

title: Rising sea levels
description: **Rising sea levels** constitute one of the major challenges of the 21st century, transforming a distant threat into a measurable physical...
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
**Rising sea levels** constitute one of the major challenges of the 21st century, transforming a distant threat into a measurable physical reality. This global phenomenon is not limited to a simple coastal overflow but results from a structural modification of the water cycle and the thermal balance of our planet.

While global ocean levels remained relatively stable for several millennia, the industrial era broke this balance, engaging a process of rise that is accelerating. With a projected elevation of **0.3 back to 1 meter** by 2100 according to greenhouse gases emission trajectories, the stability of our coastal civilizations is now being questioned.

lessons.title: The physical mechanics of elevation
lessons.content:
Ocean levels rise under the action of two distinct but complementary physical levers. The first, often misunderstood, is **Thermal expansion**. Fundamental physics teaches us that when the temperature of a liquid increases, molecular agitation intensifies, leading to an expansion of its volume. Oceans, acting as a gigantic thermal regulator, have absorbed more than **90%** of the excess heat generated by human activity since 1970. This massive absorption causes an inexorable expansion of the water column.

The second lever is the melting of ice located on land. It is imperative to distinguish <Arctic sea ice and the albedo effect> from continental ice. The melting of sea ice, which already floats on water, does not directly contribute to sea-level rise (according to Archimedes' principle). In contrast, the melting of mountain glaciers and especially **Ice sheets** - those massive polar caps resting on the bedrock of Greenland and Antarctica - pours colossal volumes of fresh water into the ocean basins.

**Greenland** alone represents a latent threat: its complete melting would raise global sea levels by **7 meters**. Although this process is slow, it has begun and is self-fueling through feedback loops that are increasingly difficult to stop.

[Greenland ice sheet melting glacier]

{Greenland is currently losing about 280 billion tons of ice per year, which is enough to cover the whole of France with a 50-centimeter layer of water every year.}

lessons.title: An acceleration of geological rhythms
lessons.content:
Historical observation shows a clear break in the kinetics of sea-level elevation. Since 1880, the global level has gained about **20 centimeters**, but it is the current speed that worries the scientific community. During most of the 20th century, the rise was about 1.4 mm/year. Today, it reaches **3.6 mm per year**, an acceleration of more than 150%.

Projections from the **IPCC** (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) indicate that this trend is irreversible in the short term due to the thermal Inertia of the oceans. Even by drastically limiting our emissions, the rise will continue. The risks are not only related to permanent submersion, but to the dramatic increase in the frequency of **chronic flooding**.

[coastal flooding sea level rise city]

Beyond the average coastline, it is **Storm surges and hundred-year floods** that devastate infrastructure. An elevation of only 50 cm in the mean level can transform a disaster supposed to happen once a century into an annual Event. This permanent instability makes the insurance and maintenance of low-lying areas economically unbearable for many states.

lessons.title: Geopolitics of submersion
lessons.content:
Rising sea levels create a deep geographical injustice: the most vulnerable areas are often those that have contributed the least to global warming. **River deltas** (Nile, Mekong, Ganges-Brahmaputra) are on the front line. In Bangladesh, where 170 million inhabitants live, a one-meter rise would cut the territory by **17%**, causing massive population displacements.

Small island states, such as the Maldives, Tuvalu, or Kiribati, face an existential threat. For these nations, the disappearance of national territory is no longer a science-fiction hypothesis but a parameter for political planning. Meanwhile, northern megacities like Miami or New York are investing billions in pump systems and dikes, creating a fracture between cities capable of financing their resilience and those condemned to retreat.

The case of **Jakarta**, in Indonesia, is emblematic. The city suffers from both rising sea levels and land subsidence due to the pumping of **groundwater tables**. Faced with the impossibility of permanently protecting the city, the government made the historic decision to build a new capital, **Nusantara**, on the island of Borneo.

[Jakarta Indonesia sinking flooding Maldives]

{The government of the Maldives held an underwater cabinet meeting in 2009, with oxygen tanks and diving suits, to sign a global call to reduce CO2 emissions before the Copenhagen conference.}

lessons.title: Towards a systemic adaptation
lessons.content:
The future of coastal areas will depend on our ability to combine two strategies: mitigating climate change to limit the rise beyond 2100, and adapting to changes that are already inevitable. Adaptation takes several forms, ranging from strengthening natural defenses (replanting **Mangroves**, dune restoration) to heavy technological solutions like the Delta Plan in the Netherlands.

However, in some cases, the solution will be **strategic retreat** or "managed relocation." This involves moving populations and economic activities inland before disasters occur repeatedly. This Concept challenges our historical attachment to the coastline, which has been the engine of globalization and urban development for three centuries.

Rising sea levels are no longer just an environmental problem; it is a global land-use planning crisis that will redefine the borders and trade routes of tomorrow. Estimates predict that about **1 billion people** will live in coastal flood zones by 2050, making international cooperation on the status of climate refugees indispensable.

|| Sea levels are currently rising by 3.6 mm/year, through the combined effect of Thermal expansion and the melting of terrestrial ice (Antarctica, Greenland). By 2100, this rise could reach 1 meter, directly threatening the existence of many island states and forcing the displacement of hundreds of millions of people living in deltas or coastal megacities. ||

quiz.question: What are the two main physical causes of sea level rise?
options: **Thermal expansion** of the oceans and the melting of continental ice (glaciers and **Ice sheets**)
Increased global precipitation and the melting of the Arctic sea ice
Air warming and the modification of deep ocean currents
The melting of floating sea ice and the accumulation of sediment at the bottom of the oceans
quiz.explanation: The rise results from the expansion of the volume of water (**expansion**) and the contribution of fresh water coming only from ice located on land (**Ice sheets** and glaciers).

quiz.question: What is the current rate of mean sea level rise?
options: About 3.6 mm per year
About 1.4 mm per year
More than 1 cm per year
Less than 0.5 mm per year
quiz.explanation: The pace has accelerated, from an average of 1.4 mm/year in the 20th century to 3.6 mm/year currently according to satellite measurements.

quiz.question: Why does the melting of sea ice not raise the water level?
options: Because it is already floating and displaces a volume of water equivalent to its weight (Archimedes' principle)
Because seawater is too salty for the melting to have an impact
Because sea ice reforms instantly during the polar winter
Because the volume of sea ice is negligible compared to the oceans
quiz.explanation: Floating ice has already displaced its volume of water; only terrestrial ice (which is added to the basin) makes the level rise when it melts.

quiz.question: Which country is planning to officially move its capital because of submersion and land subsidence?
options: Indonesia (from Jakarta to Nusantara)
Bangladesh (from Dhaka to the northern plateaus)
The Maldives (from Malé to artificial islands)
The Netherlands (from Amsterdam to Germany)
quiz.explanation: Faced with the sinking of the city and sea level rise, Indonesia is building its new capital, Nusantara, on the island of Borneo.

quiz.question: Which phenomenon increases the danger of sea level rise during storms?
options: Storm surges
The albedo effect
Subsidence
Thermal Inertia
quiz.explanation: Storm surges are temporary and sudden rises in sea level caused by low atmospheric pressure and winds during storms.

title: AI and employment
description: Does **Artificial intelligence** (AI) herald the death knell of human labor or the engine of unprecedented prosperity? This debate, which...
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
Does **Artificial intelligence** (AI) herald the death knell of human labor or the engine of unprecedented prosperity? This debate, which resurfaces with every major technological leap, takes on a singular dimension today. Unlike previous waves of automation that targeted physical strength, current AI attacks what we thought was the sanctuary of humanity: reasoning, creativity, and complex problem-solving. 

As algorithms learn and generate content at an exponential speed, the question of employment is no longer just about quantity, but about nature. This profound mutation forces us to revisit the history of labor resistance, analyze the cognitive capacities of machines, and imagine new social contracts for an era where intelligence becomes a commodity produced by silicon.

lessons.title: The legacy of resistance: from the loom to the algorithm
lessons.content:
The fear of seeing the machine supplant man is not a new phenomenon; it is consubstantial with the industrial era. At the beginning of the 19th century, the **<Luddites>**, textile workers in England, led violent actions to protest the introduction of mechanical looms that devalued their artisanal expertise.

[Luddites industrial revolution machine breaking]

Historically, technology has always followed a logic of creative destruction. The transition from agriculture to industry saw the share of farmers collapse from **40% of the working population** to only **2%** in a century in developed countries. Yet, this collapse did not lead to permanent mass unemployment, as it freed up a workforce that found its place in new sectors such as services or administration.

Each technological wave - whether steam, electricity, or computing - has had the effect of moving workers toward more complex tasks. However, generative AI seems to break this logic. For the first time, technology does not just supplement the intellectual worker; it can substitute for them in highly skilled fields.

{The term "sabotage" comes from the supposed action of French workers who threw their wooden shoes, sabots, into the machine gears to block them, although the exact origin of the word is still debated by historians.}

lessons.title: A cognitive rupture: AI facing white-collar workers
lessons.content:
**Generative AI** marks a major technological rupture because it no longer contents itself with following pre-established rules, but predicts and creates original content. Where classic computing replaced repetitive tasks (simple accounting, data entry), modern AI excels in tasks once deemed non-automatable.

[AI generative writing artificial intelligence]

Current systems are capable of analyzing complex case law, composing pieces of music, generating functional computer code, or making medical diagnoses from precision imaging. This versatility particularly exposes **<white-collar workers>**, those tertiary sector professionals whose work tool is knowledge and analysis.

According to recent reports from the **OECD** and the **IMF**, the most exposed professions now include lawyers, writers, financial analysts, and certain medical experts specialized in diagnostics. The challenge is no longer just whether AI can accomplish a task, but how much faster and less expensively it does so than a human, pushing many professions toward a radical redefinition of their value added.

{As early as 1950, Alan Turing predicted that a machine could one day simulate human thought to the point of deceiving an interlocutor. Today, some AI not only pass this test but have even been credited as co-authors of scientific patents.}

lessons.title: Recomposition and hybridization of work
lessons.content:
Despite fears of substitution, a more optimistic vision suggests that AI will act more as a co-pilot than as a replacement. By automating low-value-added tasks (documentary research, synthesis, correction), it allows professionals to focus on the relational, ethical, or strategic aspects of their profession.

[robot factory automation assembly line workers]

The emergence of new professions already testifies to this transformation. We see the appearance of **prompt engineers** (experts in the art of submitting precise instructions to AIs) or data ethics specialists. The labor market is not emptying, it is recomposing. A doctor assisted by AI does not disappear; they become capable of treating more patients with increased precision, thus reducing human errors.

However, pessimists point out that the speed of this transition is unprecedented. If past industrial revolutions spread over decades, allowing generations time to adapt, the AI revolution is unfolding in just a few years. The risk then is to see an insurmountable skills gap appear for part of the displaced workers, creating major social tensions.

{The computer term "bug" became famous when, in 1947, computer scientist Grace Hopper discovered that an actual moth (an insect) was stuck in a relay of the Mark II computer, causing a failure. She taped it into her logbook, noting: "First actual case of bug being found".}

lessons.title: Governance and the future of the value of work
lessons.content:
The outcome of this upheaval will depend less on the technology itself than on the political and social choices that will frame it. To mitigate the effects of mass automation, several avenues are being explored by governments and economists. Continuous training becomes an absolute necessity to allow a fluid transition toward new skills.

Furthermore, the debate on the redistribution of wealth produced by machines is reignited. If AI allows for producing more with less labor, how do we finance our social models? It is in this context that the idea of a **<universal basic income (UBI)>** gains credibility, no longer as a utopia, but as a safety net for a society where human work would no longer be the only source of income.

There is also talk of implementing taxation on robots or the use of artificial intelligence to compensate for the loss of social contributions linked to work. Ultimately, AI forces us to rethink the place of work in human identity and to envision a future where productivity would no longer be synonymous with painful human effort.

|| Previous industrial revolutions destroyed jobs while creating others - generative AI is the first to simultaneously threaten cognitive and creative tasks. ||

quiz.question: Who were the Luddites, and why is their Movement cited in the debate on AI?
options: English weavers from the 19th century who destroyed textile machines
German philosophers who theorized the end of work in the 18th century
French artisans fighting against the industrial manufacture of clogs
A British automotive union opposed to robotization in 1970
quiz.explanation: The Luddites (1811-1816) are the historical symbol of worker resistance against mechanization that threatened their wages and skills.

quiz.question: How does the impact of Generative AI differ from historical automations?
options: It automates cognitive and creative tasks once reserved for humans
It only concerns physical and repetitive jobs in industry
It requires no energy resources to operate
It is the first technology to create only precarious jobs
quiz.explanation: Unlike industrial robots, Generative AI can write, code, and create, directly impacting intellectual professions (white-collar workers).

quiz.question: Which Event of 2023 illustrates the tension between AI and creative professions?
options: The simultaneous strike of Hollywood writers and actors
The takeover of Twitter by Elon Musk to turn it into an AI
The massive closure of advertising agencies in Paris
The global boycott of tablet drawing software
quiz.explanation: In 2023, American writers and actors went on strike notably to obtain guarantees against the replacement of their work by Generative AI.

quiz.question: Which trend does the World Economic Forum highlight for the future of work?
options: The displacement of millions of jobs offset by the creation of new roles
The total disappearance of human work in favor of machines by 2030
A massive return to manual agricultural trades without technology
Absolute stability of the labor market without any job creation
quiz.explanation: The Forum anticipates a major transition (85M jobs displaced versus 97M created), highlighting the importance of professional retraining.

quiz.question: Which economic solution is often proposed to counter the risk of technological unemployment?
options: Universal basic income
The total ban of computers in companies
The reduction of working time to 10 hours per week
The return to the Gold standard to limit investments in AI
quiz.explanation: Universal basic income is proposed as a safety net to decouple income from automated human productivity.

title: Populism: why is it rising everywhere?
description: **Populism** is no longer a marginal phenomenon but a driving force transforming global balances since the 2010s. From the United States with...
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: **Populism** is no longer a marginal phenomenon but a driving force transforming global balances since the 2010s. From the United States with **Trumpism** to Central Europe, from Latin America to India, leaders are shaking up established party structures. Far from being a simple electoral whim, populism is rooted in deep fractures - economic, cultural, and technological - that challenge the permanence of the liberal democracy model. This course explores the mechanics of this discourse, its structural causes, and its consequences on the organization of contemporary powers.

lessons.title: Binary logic: a pure people versus a corrupt elite
lessons.content:
**Populism** is not defined by a precise economic program, but by a specific **political logic**. According to political scientist **Jan-Werner Müller**, its fundamental characteristic is **monism**: the idea that there is only one "true people" of whom the leader is the only legitimate spokesperson. This vision divides society into two hostile and homogeneous blocks: on one side, the **"pure people"**, holders of instinctive wisdom and authentic values; on the other, the **"corrupt elite"**, accused of betraying the general interest in favor of hidden agendas or financial interests.

[populist political rally crowd flags]

This discursive structure is highly adaptable. On the right, the "people" are often defined by national or ethnic identity, opposed to a "globalist" elite or minorities perceived as threats. On the left, they are defined by social class (the "99%") against the financial oligarchy. 

Populism is by nature **anti-pluralist**. By claiming to embody the entirety of the popular will, the populist leader disqualifies political opponents not as legitimate competitors, but as enemies of the people. This posture often justifies questioning intermediate institutions - Justice, the press, independent bodies - perceived as obstacles to the direct expression of sovereignty.

{Historically, the first major modern populist party, the American People's Party in 1892, called for the nationalization of railroads because farmers felt that rates were set by an invisible financial 'elite'.}

lessons.title: The drivers of anger: economy and identity
lessons.content:
The rise of populist movements results from the convergence of several crises. On the economic front, the Concept of the **elephant curve**, theorized by **Branko Milanović**, illustrates the effects of **globalization**. This curve shows that while Asian middle classes and the global ultra-rich saw their incomes explode between 1988 and 2008, Western middle and working classes suffered a brutal stagnation. This downgrading, real or felt, fueled a sense of abandonment compared to dynamic urban centers.

[2015 refugee migration crisis Europe Mediterranean]

Added to this economic fracture is a deep **cultural divide**. The acceleration of societal changes (minority rights, secularization) and the impact of the **migration crisis** have generated identity insecurity. For many voters, political elites are perceived as closer to global concerns than to local realities. This phenomenon of cultural **backlash** favors discourses advocating a return to strong national sovereignty and traditional values.

Finally, the digital revolution has transformed political communication. **Social networks** act as echo chambers that reinforce polarization. They allow leaders to bypass **mass media** to address their base directly, often using emotional and simplified language that breaks free from usual fact-checking.

{The concept of the 'echo chamber' was not born with the Internet: it comes from architectural acoustics where certain domes reflect sound in such a way that one only hears one's own voice, isolating the individual from outside noises.}

lessons.title: Geography and faces of contemporary populism
lessons.content:
The global political landscape offers a gallery of figures illustrating the diversity of the phenomenon. **Donald Trump** transformed the American Republican Party into a populist Movement focused on protectionism and nationalism. In Europe, **Viktor Orbán** in Hungary has become the architect of **illiberal democracies**, a model where elections justify the concentration of power in the hands of the executive at the expense of the rule of law.

[Donald Trump Marine Le Pen populist leaders]

In France, **Marine Le Pen** has undertaken a strategy of <normalization> to broaden her electoral base, while maintaining a core centered on national preference and opposition to the European Union. Populist influence is also found in **Giorgia Meloni** in Italy or **Jair Bolsonaro** in Brazil, often sharing a skepticism toward multilateral institutions and hostility toward global environmental discourses.

Left-wing populism, represented by figures like **Jean-Luc Mélenchon** in France or **Bernie Sanders** in the United States, prioritizes the redistribution of wealth and the fight against monopolies. Although their goals differ radically from right-wing populists, they share the same rhetoric of breaking with the "system" and the desire to restore power to the popular vote against the constraints of financial markets.

lessons.title: The challenges of exercising power
lessons.content:
The great paradox of populism appears when it gains responsibility. Once in government, the populist can no longer be content with being the opponent of the system; he becomes the system. To maintain his image as a rebel, he must often designate new enemies (judges, civil servants, foreign powers) who would prevent the application of his will.

This is where the risk to institutions becomes tangible. The exercise of populist power tends to weaken **checks and balances**. In Hungary or Poland (under the PiS government), reforms aimed to limit the independence of the judiciary. In the event of electoral defeat, some leaders contest the very **Legitimacy** of the vote, as illustrated by the Capitol attack in 2021 or the events in Brasilia in 2023, thus threatening the principle of the peaceful transition of power.

However, the rise of populism also acts as a wake-up call for liberal democracies. It forces traditional parties to reclaim neglected subjects, such as industrial sovereignty or the protection of public services in rural areas. The response to populism lies not only in moral condemnation, but in the capacity of institutions to prove their effectiveness in the face of the daily concerns of citizens.

|| Populism divides the World into a "pure people" against a "corrupt elite" - it has been rising everywhere since 2010, driven by inequalities linked to globalization and cultural insecurity amplified by social networks. ||

{One of the most popular presidents of the United States, Andrew Jackson (1829), was nicknamed 'King Mob' by his detractors because he had opened the White House to the people for a party that ended in a near-riot.}

quiz.question: According to the political scientist's definition, what is the central characteristic of populist discourse?
options: The "pure people" opposed to a "corrupt elite"
The systematic refusal of any nuance in politics
The intensive use of social media
Broad promises of simple solutions to all problems
quiz.explanation: Populism is defined by this binary vision of society separating so-called 'authentic' citizens from an elite accused of corruption or betrayal.

quiz.question: According to Jan-Werner Müller, what makes populism fundamentally "anti-pluralist"?
options: The populist claims to be the only legitimate representative of the "true people"
The populist refuses democratic debate organized by institutions
The populist rejects any political compromise on principle
The populist openly despises all representative institutions
quiz.explanation: By claiming to be the sole spokesperson for the people, the populist de facto denies the legitimacy of any opposition, a principle that is nevertheless central to democratic pluralism.

quiz.question: What does Milanović's “elephant curve” show regarding Western economic anxiety?
options: Western middle classes have seen their incomes stagnate while emerging countries and the wealthiest progressed
Emerging countries have caught up with the West in terms of overall GDP
Globalization has impoverished 99% of the population in developed countries
Growth only benefits the richest 10% on the planet
quiz.explanation: This curve illustrates that the relative big losers of globalization are the working and middle classes of Western democracies, which creates fertile ground for populism.

quiz.question: What common theme is found among right-wing populists such as Trump, Orbán, or Le Pen?
options: Anti-immigration, cultural nationalism, and hostility toward perceived elites
A military past, as all are former career officers
A desire to systematically exit all international organizations
The exclusive use of paper newspapers for their communication
quiz.explanation: These leaders share a rhetoric focused on protecting national identity against external influences (migration, globalization) and the rejection of elite structures.

quiz.question: How can populism weaken the rule of law once in power?
options: By eroding checks and balances such as an independent judiciary and a free press
By increasing the number of referendums on all societal issues
By completely abolishing the voting rights of opponents
By nationalizing the country's entire economy
quiz.explanation: Populism in power tends to weaken the institutions that limit the executive branch, as it views them as illegitimate obstacles to the will of the people as defined by the leader.

title: Mental health as a societal issue
description: Long sidelined to the margins of traditional medicine, **mental health** is now emerging as one of the major challenges of the 21st century. It...
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: Long sidelined to the margins of traditional medicine, **mental health** is now emerging as one of the major challenges of the 21st century. It defines not only the absence of psychiatric disorders, but a state of well-being allowing everyone to realize their potential and cope with the normal difficulties of life. Yet, a striking paradox remains: while these disorders represent about **20% of the global burden of disease**, they capture on average only **2% of national health budgets**. This asymmetry between the need for care and public investment outlines the contours of a global health crisis often described as a silent epidemic. From clinical depression to professional burnout, the constant increase in diagnoses calls for a profound overhaul of our social and economic models.

lessons.title: The silent epidemic: a global public health crisis
lessons.content:
The rise of mental disorders is redefining the hierarchy of health threats. Today, **depression** has risen to the rank of the leading cause of disability worldwide, surpassing cardiovascular diseases or diabetes in terms of years of life lost or disability. This pathology, characterized by persistent sadness and loss of interest, affects all segments of the population, but remains underdiagnosed in many geographic areas.

[depression mental health person dark]

Beyond depression, generalized **anxiety** affects about 300 million people, creating a state of chronic worry that paralyzes daily functioning. This psychic distress sometimes culminates in the ultimate act: **suicide**, which is responsible for **700,000 people per year** in the World. This terrifying figure exceeds the total number of victims of wars and natural disasters combined, highlighting the structural failure of current prevention systems.

Institutional recognition is nonetheless progressing. In 2019, the WHO took a symbolic step by integrating <burnout> into the International Classification of Diseases, not as a disease in itself, but as a "work-related phenomenon". This distinction is crucial: it shifts the responsibility from the individual alone to their organizational environment.

{The word "melancholy" comes from the Ancient Greek 'melankholía', which literally means "black bile". In Antiquity, it was thought that depression was caused by an excess of this liquid in the body.}

lessons.title: The generational shift: the impact of digital technology
lessons.content:
While the entire population is vulnerable, the situation of **adolescents and young adults** is of particular concern. In the United States, anxiety and depression indicators among 12-25 year olds have seen a staggering increase, almost doubling in a decade. Researchers agree on the existence of a major chronological break located around **2012**.

[teenagers smartphones social media anxiety]

This Date corresponds to the massive generalization of the smartphone and the explosion of social media use. Psychologist **Jean Twenge** argues that this technological transition has radically modified the temporal and social structure of youth. The shift from physical sociability to permanent digital interaction has favored several deleterious mechanisms. On one hand, Upward social comparison, where young people measure themselves against unrealistic living and beauty standards, generates a feeling of profound inadequacy. On the other hand, Cyber-victimization and chronic sleep disruption by the blue light of screens exacerbate emotional vulnerability.

Social networks like **Instagram** or **TikTok** act as echo chambers for psychological insecurity. The attention economy, which governs these platforms, relies on loops of Dopaminergic reinforcement that can induce addictive behaviors, diverting individuals from protective activities like sport or restorative sleep.

lessons.title: Economic stakes and institutional responses
lessons.content:
The impact of mental health is not limited to the private sphere; it infiltrates the heart of economic productivity. It is estimated that the annual cost related to burnout and suffering at work amounts to **$300 billion per year** in the United States alone. This cost encompasses absenteeism, turnover (permanent staff renewal), and presenteeism, a situation where the employee is physically present but psychically unable to work effectively.

[workplace burnout stress mental health]

Faced with this financial abyss, companies are beginning to integrate well-being and prevention programs. However, at the state level, the challenge remains intact, particularly in low- or middle-income countries where access to a psychiatrist or psychologist is almost non-existent. To respond to this issue, the WHO launched a global action plan aiming to reduce the Treatment gap, by integrating mental health care into primary health services.

One of the most powerful levers for change remains destigmatization. When public figures, such as Simone Biles, speak openly about their difficulties, they contribute to transforming a "mark of weakness" into a legitimate health issue. This cultural shift is essential to encourage patients to consult earlier.

lessons.title: Toward a new social contract for mental health
lessons.content:
The future of mental health will depend on our ability to move from curative medicine - which treats the symptom once the crisis has occurred - to an environmental and preventive approach. This implies rethinking urban planning, education, and work rhythm to minimize systemic stressors. The emergence of digital therapies and Artificial intelligence in psychiatric monitoring offers new perspectives to fill the lack of practitioners, although these tools raise major ethical questions about the confidentiality of sensitive data.

Mental health is now inseparable from ecological and political issues. The Concept of Eco-anxiety, for example, illustrates how global threats directly impact the individual psyche. Ultimately, the recognition of mental health as a fundamental human right and a pillar of the stability of nations is the necessary condition for facing the crises to come.

quiz.question: What percentage of the global burden of disease do mental disorders represent according to the WHO?
options: About 20% of global morbidity
About 5% of global morbidity
About 30% of global morbidity
About 10% of global morbidity
quiz.explanation: According to the WHO, mental disorders represent one-fifth (20%) of the global burden of disease, although they are largely underfunded.

quiz.question: What factor does Jean Twenge identify as the trigger for the mental health crisis among young people in 2012?
options: The widespread adoption of smartphones and social media
The European economic euro crisis
The tightening of international school systems
The increase in urban air pollution
quiz.explanation: The course specifies that 2012 marks the tipping point where the massive adoption of smartphones transformed teenage sociability towards the digital realm.

quiz.question: What is the estimated economic consequence of burnout for American companies?
options: An annual cost of $300 billion
An annual cost of $50 billion
An annual cost of $1 trillion
An annual cost of $100 billion
quiz.explanation: Burnout impacts the economy through absenteeism and reduced productivity, representing a massive cost of $300 billion per year in the USA.

quiz.question: Which institutional body officially recognized burnout as a work-related phenomenon in 2019?
options: The World Health Organization (WHO)
The International Labour Organization (ILO)
The United Nations (UN)
The European Court of Human Rights
quiz.explanation: The WHO included burnout in its international classification in 2019, allowing for better recognition of suffering at work.

quiz.question: What is the term for the mechanism where an individual feels diminished when faced with filtered images on social media?
options: Upward social comparison
Dopaminergic reinforcement
Systemic eco-anxiety
Digital depersonalization
quiz.explanation: Upward social comparison refers to comparing oneself to models perceived as superior, which harms self-esteem among young people.

title: The EU: how does it really work?
description: The **European Union** represents the most successful experience of supranational integration in modern history, transforming a continent ravaged...
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The **European Union** represents the most successful experience of supranational integration in modern history, transforming a continent ravaged by wars into an integrated economic and politics bloc. Yet, its inner workings are often perceived as a bureaucratic "black box" by the 450 million citizens it governs. 

Far from being a classic federal state, the EU relies on a complex balance of powers where no actor can decide alone. Understanding how decisions are made in Brussels, from the initial idea to the law applicable in each State, makes it possible to decode major contemporary issues, from the ecological transition to digital sovereignty.

lessons.title: The institutional triangle: who really decides?
lessons.content:
The architecture of the EU is based on what is called the **institutional triangle**, a system of checks and balances between national interests and the general European interest. At the top of the political impulse is the **European Council**, composed of heads of state or government. It is here, during the Brussels summits, that the major strategic directions are set without, however, legislating directly.

[European Council leaders Brussels summit]

The legislative power is then shared between two bodies: the **<Council of the EU>** (or Council of Ministers) which represents the governments of the 27 Member States, and the **European Parliament**, the only institution whose members are directly elected by universal suffrage. The latter ensures the democratic legitimacy of the system, although it does not yet have a full right of legislative initiative.

[European Parliament Strasbourg hemicycle]

Finally, the **<European Commission>** acts as the executive body. It holds the monopoly on the initiative law, which means that no measure can be discussed without it having proposed it. It is also the "guardian of the treaties", responsible for prosecuting States that do not respect common law. This institutional editing ensures that no law is adopted without the cross-agreement of a majority of States and a majority of representatives of the citizens.

{The European Parliament has two official seats: Brussels and Strasbourg. Every month, the 705 MEPs and all their staff move by special train to Alsace for a four-day plenary session, a costly ritual symbolizing Franco-German reconciliation.}

lessons.title: The law factory: from proposal to application
lessons.content:
The process of creating a European norm mostly follows the **ordinary legislative procedure**, formerly called co-decision. Everything starts with a proposal from the European Commission, often resulting from a long phase of consultation with experts and <interest groups>.

The text is then transmitted to the Parliament and the Council of the EU. These two institutions examine the project in "first reading". They can approve it as is, or more frequently, propose amendments. If the two institutions do not agree, a **shuttle** is organized. As a last resort, a <conciliation committee> is convened to seal a political compromise.

Once adopted, legislation can take two main legal forms: the **regulation**, which applies directly and uniformly in all Member States as soon as it is published, and the **directive**, which sets objectives to be achieved but leaves the States the choice of form and means to transpose them into their national law. This system allows the EU to harmonize the single market while respecting the legal specificities of each nation. This process, although slow, ensures legal robustness through the control of the **Court of Justice of the European Union** (CJEU), which ensures that no one deviates from the common rule.

{The Court of Justice has had to settle unusual conflicts, such as the famous "banana war" which lasted more than 20 years, pitting the EU against the United States over customs duties applied to tropical fruits.}

lessons.title: Fields of action and limits of sovereignty
lessons.content:
The EU does not possess unlimited authority; it is governed by the principle of **conferral**, only being able to act where the States have delegated competence to it. Three levels of action can be distinguished. **Exclusive competences** concern areas where only the EU can legislate, such as the customs union, trade policy or the management of the single currency for eurozone countries.

The second level is that of **shared competences**. This is the heart of Brussels' activity, covering the environment, transport or consumer protection. Here the principle of **subsidiarity** applies: the EU only intervenes if its action is deemed more effective than that of isolated States.

[EU flag stars Brussels institutions]

Finally, certain areas remain jealously guarded by national capitals: this is the case for **direct taxation**, **health** or **defense**. In these sectors of vital importance for sovereignty, decisions often require unanimity. It is this lock that explains why the EU can impose record fines on tech giants (commercial competence), but sometimes struggles to agree on a common diplomacy in the face of a global geopolitical crisis.

{The European anthem, taken from Beethoven's Ode to Joy, features no official lyrics. This is a deliberate choice so as not to favor one European language over others.}

lessons.title: Challenges and realities of European governance
lessons.content:
The image of a Europe run by "unelected technocrats" is a recurring criticism that deserves to be nuanced. Although the Commissioners are not directly elected, they are appointed by governments resulting from democratic elections and must be validated by the European Parliament. Furthermore, the European civil service is relatively small: with around 60,000 agents across all institutions, the EU employs fewer civil servants than the city of Paris to administer an entire continent.

However, the challenge of the **democratic deficit** persists. The complexity of procedures and the geographical distance from Brussels create a sense of disconnection. To address this, the EU introduced the **European Citizens' Initiative** (ECI), allowing one million citizens to ask the Commission to propose legislation on a specific subject.

The future of the Union is being played out today on its ability to react to rapid crises. The 2020 pandemic marked a historic turning point with the **Next Generation EU** plan, where for the first time, Member States agreed to borrow together on the financial markets. This transition from a union of markets to a union of financial solidarity outlines the contours of deeper integration, despite persistent tensions over respect for rule of law values by certain members.

|| The European Union is a unique co-decision system where 27 States agree to share their sovereignty to have more weight in globalization, guaranteed peace and stability through the rule of law. ||

quiz.question: Which internal EU Institution holds the monopoly on legislative initiative?
options: The European Commission
The European Parliament
The European Council
The Court of Justice of the EU
quiz.explanation: According to the treaties, only the Commission can formally propose a piece of Law, although the Parliament or the Council may invite it to do so.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between a European "regulation" and a "directive"?
options: The regulation applies directly, whereas the directive must be transposed by each State
The regulation is optional, the directive is mandatory
The regulation only concerns the economy, the directive concerns social issues
The directive applies faster than the regulation
quiz.explanation: The regulation is of immediate and uniform application. The directive sets an objective but leaves member States the freedom regarding the legal method to achieve it.

quiz.question: What does the principle of "subsidiarity" stipulate in European Union law?
options: The EU only acts if its action is more effective than that carried out at the national level
The EU is superior to States in all sovereign domains
States must fully fund European projects
Only the European Parliament can cancel a national law
quiz.explanation: Subsidiarity ensures that decisions are taken as close as possible to the citizens, with the EU only intervening for matters requiring a continental scale.

quiz.question: Approximately how many civil servants does the EU employ to administer its 450 million citizens?
options: About 60,000 civil servants
More than 500,000 civil servants
About 1 million civil servants
Fewer than 5,000 civil servants
quiz.explanation: Despite the image of a bloated bureaucracy, the European administration is proportionally one of the smallest in the world per inhabitant.

quiz.question: Which body sets the major political priorities without, however, voting on laws?
options: The European Council
The European Commission
The Council of the EU
The European Central Bank
quiz.explanation: The European Council, which brings together Heads of State or Government, provides the political impetus but does not technically participate in the legislative process.

title: Press freedom around the world
description: **Press freedom** constitutes one of the most precise thermometers of a nation's democratic health. It is not limited to the right to publish, but...
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content: **Press freedom** constitutes one of the most precise thermometers of a nation's democratic health. It is not limited to the right to publish, but encompasses the ability of citizens to access plural, verified information independent of those in power. However, the contemporary media landscape is under double pressure: an unprecedented authoritarian offensive in dictatorial regimes and a disintegration of protection structures in liberal democracies. Understanding these mechanisms is essential to grasping the issues of digital sovereignty and opinion manipulation that characterize the 21st century.

lessons.title: The erosion of global democratic guarantees
lessons.content:
The global information panorama is marked by growing hostility. Every year, the organization <Reporters Without Borders> (RSF) publishes its reference report to map the obstacles to the exercise of the journalism profession.

[press freedom world map RSF index]

**2024** data reveals an alarming reality: less than **10%** of the World's population resides in an area where the press operates without hindrance. While Scandinavian countries (Norway, Denmark) maintain high standards thanks to strong legislative protection and a culture of transparency, vast territories are tipping into zones of silence. **China**, **Russia**, **Iran**, or **Myanmar** are among the most hostile environments, where the exercise of investigative journalism is systematically equated with treason or espionage.

Repression manifests through direct physical violence. In **2023**, at least **79 journalists** lost their lives in the line of duty, often deliberately targeted to silence troublesome investigations. At the same time, judicial harassment is becoming a favored weapon of control, with nearly **600 journalists** imprisoned annually across the globe.

[journalist arrested press freedom protest]

{Turkmenistan is one of the Rare countries in the World where the State controls information so rigorously that it officially banned the word "coronavirus" from the media and health brochures at the start of the 2020 pandemic.}

lessons.title: The weakening of Western democratic models
lessons.content:
Contrary to popular belief, press freedom is not a definitive achievement in Western countries. It is undergoing worrying mutations there, no longer through direct State Censorship, but through mechanisms of <media concentration> and financial influence. The massive buyout of press titles by industrial conglomerates or billionaires poses a major challenge to editorial independence.

In **Hungary**, under the government of <Viktor Orbán>, a sophisticated strategy was put in place: rather than banning opposition media, the power favored their buyout by oligarchs close to the party, transforming the media landscape into a government echo chamber through institutional advertising. This model of media capture inspires other populist leaders across Europe.

In **France**, the debate crystallizes around the concentration of media in the hands of a few large groups. This situation raises fears of the emergence of editorial self-censorship, anxious not to offend the economic interests of their shareholders. Furthermore, countries like **India** or **Greece** are seeing the use of spyware and abusive legal procedures (<SLAPP>) multiply to intimidate critical voices, proving that digital surveillance has become a cross-border tool of repression.

{The concept of "gonzo" journalism, where the reporter becomes the protagonist of their own story, was popularized by Hunter S. Thompson who claimed: "Fiction is often closer to the truth than objective journalism."}

lessons.title: The economic crisis and the survival of information
lessons.content:
Beyond political threats, journalism is going through a **structural economic crisis** that threatens its very viability. The historical model based on newsstand sales and advertising broke with the advent of digital. Today, dominant platforms capture almost all online advertising growth, depriving newsrooms of their financial oxygen.

[newspaper crisis digital transformation journalism]

This scarcity of resources leads to the closure of many local newspapers, creating "information deserts" where no check on the actions of local elected officials or businesses remains. Faced with this danger, new economic models are emerging. Public interest journalism is increasingly turning to non-profit structures, funded by patronage or direct subscriptions.

Titles like **Mediapart** in France or **ProPublica** in the United States demonstrate that it is possible to build a profitable model by placing independence at the heart of the editorial promise. However, these models require an engaged and solvent readership, which raises the question of access to quality information for the entire population, in the face of the proliferation of free content that is often unreliable or partisan.

{The first printed newspaper in History, the "Relation," was launched in Strasbourg in 1605 by Johann Carolus, long before the invention of legal press freedom.}

lessons.title: Digital challenges and the ethics of the future
lessons.content:
The digital age has radically transformed the speed of information dissemination, but it has also generated new dangers such as systemic <disinformation>. Social media algorithms tend to favor emotional and divisive content over factual analysis, creating filter bubbles that fragment **collective memory**.

The journalist's role is therefore evolving from one of simple broadcaster to that of a "certifier" of reality. Professional Ethics is more than ever called upon in the face of the incessant flow of images and data. Respect for image rights and human dignity often constitute complex moral dilemmas, as illustrated by <Ethics of photojournalism> in conflict or famine zones.

Defending press freedom will necessarily involve international regulation of digital platforms and reinforced media education for citizens. Without a free press capable of challenging official narratives and verifying facts, the democratic social contract risks dissolving into a relativism where all opinions are equal, regardless of their truth.

quiz.question: According to RSF (Reporters Without Borders), what proportion of the global population lives in a country where the press is truly free?
options: Less than 10% of the world population
About 30%

title: Climate migration
description: The **climate change** is no longer just an environmental threat; it is a driver of unprecedented demographic transformations. In the coming...
subject: comprendreLeMonde

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.content:
The **climate change** is no longer just an environmental threat; it is a driver of unprecedented demographic transformations. In the coming decades, hundreds of millions of people will be forced to abandon their homes, driven out by Rising sea levels, galloping desertification, or extreme heat phenomena making certain territories unlivable. 

These **Climate migration** patterns represent one of the most complex challenges of the 21st century, as they mix human rights issues, national security, and metaphysical justice. As flows intensify, the World faces a fundamental question: how can populations displaced by global causes be protected when international law remains frozen in national definitions inherited from the post-war era?

lessons.title: The scale of contemporary demographic shock
lessons.content:
Climate migration is not a matter of distant forecasting: it is an immediate statistical reality. In **2022**, data revealed a symbolic tipping point: the number of **internal displacements** (population movements within a single country) linked to climate disasters reached **60 million**. For the first time in modern History, this figure surpasses that of people fleeing armed conflicts, highlighting that nature has become a more powerful destabilizing agent than war.

The long-term trajectory is even more alarming. The **World Bank**, in its reference reports, estimates that if no radical measures for emissions reduction and adaptation are taken, climate change could force **216 million people** to migrate by **2050**. These movements are mostly concentrated in areas of high geographic vulnerability.

**Bangladesh**, a country of deltas, illustrates the frontal attack of the ocean: the combination of Rising sea levels and the violence of cyclones reduces arable land every year. In **Sub-Saharan Africa**, it is the disappearance of water resources that pushes rural populations toward already saturated metropolises. Finally, the small **Low-lying island states** of the Pacific face an existential threat: the total submersion of their national territory by the horizon of 2100.

[Bangladesh flooding climate refugees]

{ In 2009, the government of the Maldives held an underwater cabinet meeting, with oxygen tanks and diving suits, to alert the World to the imminent disappearance of their archipelago below sea level.}

lessons.title: Mechanisms of disruption: disasters and slow-onset degradation
lessons.content:
To understand migratory dynamics, one must distinguish between two types of environmental temporalities. On one hand, **sudden disasters**, such as tropical storms or landslides, cause brutal and spectacular exoduses. These movements are often temporary: populations attempt to return and rebuild on-site once the hazard has passed, although the repetition of shocks eventually erodes this resilience.

On the other hand, **slow-onset degradation** transforms ecosystems irreversibly. Rising sea levels do not just submerge coasts; they cause the salinization of groundwater tables, making agriculture impossible long before the water reaches homes. Similarly, desertification gradually transforms grazing areas into sterile lands, forcing pastoral communities into <Forced settlement> or urban exile.

[Sahel drought desertification climate Africa]

A new and terrifying factor is now emerging: **wet-bulb heat**. When temperature and humidity exceed a certain threshold (a wet-bulb temperature of 35°C), the human body can no longer dissipate its own heat through perspiration. By 2050, densely populated areas of the Persian Gulf and South Asia could become physiologically lethal for any human being remaining outside for more than a few hours, causing absolute survival migrations.

lessons.title: The legal impasse and the legal vacuum
lessons.content:
Despite the evidence of the crisis, people displaced by the climate fall into a gaping <Legal vacuum of the "climate refugee">. The term "climate refugee," though commonly used by media and NGOs, has no value in international law. The **1951 Geneva Convention**, which defines refugee status, was designed to protect individuals persecuted by their own state for political, racial, or religious reasons. However, climate change is not a targeted persecution, but a systemic global phenomenon.

Without this official status, climate migrants do not benefit from the principle of **non-refoulement**, which prohibits a country from returning a person to a territory where their life is in danger. This creates a profound injustice: the most vulnerable countries, such as Bangladesh or the Sahel states, are historically the **least responsible** for greenhouse gases emissions. Conversely, industrialized nations, whose development relied on fossil fuels, have the financial capacity to adapt but often strengthen their migratory closure policies.

[climate refugees displaced people camp]

This situation fuels the Concept of **climate debt**: the idea that Northern countries have a moral and financial obligation to assume the human consequences of warming, including hosting populations whose habitat has become physically unlivable because of this development model.

lessons.title: Towards recognition and global management
lessons.content:
The future of Climate migration will depend on our ability to invent new frameworks of cooperation. Some countries are attempting pioneering solutions. <Low-lying island states> are exploring, for example, the notion of sovereignty without territory: how can one remain a nation recognized at the UN if the physical island has disappeared? Kiribati has, in fact, purchased land in Fiji to ensure food security and a possible relocation of its population.

At the international level, the 2018 **Global Compact for Migration** is timidly beginning to mention environmental factors as causes of displacement. However, most experts agree that the priority must remain **local adaptation**: investing in dikes, salt-resistant crops, and early warning systems to allow people to stay in their homes. For migration, when forced rather than chosen, is always perceived as an admission of failure in development policies.

The migration issue is thus the mirror of our failure to stabilize the climate. If flows become massive and disorderly, they risk causing major geopolitical tensions, particularly over access to water and habitable land. Managing these displacements is no longer a humanitarian option, but a necessity for global stability in the coming century.

|| To remember: In 2022, climate disasters caused 60 million internal displacements, surpassing war refugees. Without an international legal status (vacuum of the Geneva Convention), these populations remain without protection in the face of a crisis that could involve 216 million people by 2050. ||
